According to recent reports, AAV2-CAG-DIO-membrane bound YFP (AAV-CAG-DIO-mYFP, Addgene ID 263586) was modified from AAV-EF1a-BbTagBY (Addgene ID 45185). AAV serotype 2 was produced at 2 × 1013 vg ml−1 and used in combination with Cre-driver mouse lines to selectively label axons of defined RGC starter populations. This enabled visualization of cell-type-specific RGC axonal projections in SC.

The brain preparation for TransA-MERFISH was optimized to preserve immunohistochemical staining and maximize RNA quality for subsequent RNA multiplexing experiments. Young adult mice were deeply anaesthetized and transcardially perfused with ice-cold saline (0.9% NaCl solution), followed by ice-cold 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) in 0.1 M phosphate buffer (pH 7.4). After dissection, the brains were post-fixed in the same fixative solution overnight at 4 °C. The target brain regions (SC in this study, about 10 mm3 in volume) were micro-dissected, with anteroposterior and dorsoventral orientations carefully marked. This was followed by cryoprotection in 30% sucrose in PBS at 4 °C until the tissues sank (2–4 h). The target regions were embedded in OCT compound and rapidly frozen in a dry ice-cooled 2-methylbutane (Supelco, MX0760-1). Then, approximately 12 µm coronal sections were prepared on a cryostat and collected under RNase-free conditions on MERSCOPE Slides (Vizgen) for RNA-grade processing.

Industry observers note that for each mouse, about 10 coronal sections were obtained using the right SC, which receives contralateral retinal input from the left eye injected with mWmC tracer, from the perfusion–fixation protocol described above. Sections were collected at intervals of every 9 slices (12 µm each, totalling about 100 µm), spanning the anterior-to-posterior axis of the right SC. The coronal sections encompassing the SC were selected based on the Allen Mouse Brain Atlas, corresponding to stereotaxic coordinates relative to Bregma ranging from −3.0 mm to −5.0 mm. The section captures the full dorsoventral extent of the SC, from the superficial visual layers stratum zonale (SZ), SGS, to deep motor-associated layers stratum griseum profundum (SGP) and stratum album profundum (SAP).

The SC tissues on MERSLIDES (Vizgen, 20400001) were first permeablized in 70% ethanol (4°C) overnight, followed by a series of ethanol gradient dehydration: 90% ethanol at room temperature for 5 min, 100% ethanol at room temperature for 1 h, 90% ethanol at room temperature for 5 min, and then incubated with 70% ethanol at room temperature for 5 min. SC sections were then prepared for MERSCOPE imaging using the MERSCOPE Sample Preparation Kit (Vizgen, 10400012) and following the MERSCOPE User Guide (Fresh and Fixed Frozen Tissue Sample Preparation, 91600002 RevF).

Sources indicate that for protein staining, the sample was washed with 5 ml of PBS. Blocking solution (10:1 Blocking Buffer C Premix: RNase inhibitor) (Blocking Buffer C, Vizgen 20300100; RNase inhibitor Murine, NEB M0314L) was then added to the centre of the tissue section and incubated at room temperature for 1 h. The sample was incubated in Primary Staining Solution (100:10:1 Blocking Buffer C Premix: RNase inhibitor: Primary antibody) at room temperature for 1 h. Notably, anti-RFP (rabbit, Rockland 46510) was diluted 1:100 for this step. The sample was subsequently washed with PBS. Secondary Staining Solution (100:10:3:1 Blocking Buffer Premix: RNase inhibitor: Secondary Stain Mix : Protein Stain) (Anti-Rabbit Protein Stain Kit, Vizgen, 10400107) was then added to the sample and incubated for 1 h. The sample was then washed with PBS. Fixation Buffer (4% PFA in PBS) was then added to the tissue section, and the section was incubated at room temperature for 15 min. The sample was then washed with PBS.

In a recent development, next, for encoding probe hybridization, the sample was incubated in 5 ml Formamide Wash Buffer (Vizgen, 20300002) at 37 °C for 30 min. The Formamide Wash Buffer was then carefully aspirated, and the custom 140-Gene MERSCOPE Gene Panel Mix (Vizgen, VZG180, mouse superficial SC panel; Supplementary Table 1) was added to the tissue section, which was then incubated in a humidified chamber at 37 °C for at least 36 h and up to 48 h. Then, in the post-encoding probe hybridization washes, Formamide Wash Buffer was added to the sample and incubated at 47 °C for 30 min. This wash step was repeated, then the sample was incubated in the Sample Prep Wash Buffer (Vizgen, 20300001) for 2 min.

Then for gel embedding, wash buffer was aspirated from the MERSLIDE, and Gel Embedding Solution (2:10:1 Gel Embedding Premix: 10% w/v ammonium persulfate solution: N,N,N′,N′-tetramethylethylenediamine) (Gel Embedding Premix, Vizgen 20300004; ammonium persulfate, Sigma-Aldrich 09913; N,N,N′,N′-tetramethylethylenediamine, Sigma-Aldrich T7024) was added to cover the tissue sections. A coverslip pretreated with Gel Slick (VWR, 12001-812) was placed directly over the tissue sections and incubated at room temperature for 90 min to allow the gel to solidify. The coverslip was then removed. Then, the sample was treated to clear it. The sample was incubated in a pre-warmed Clearing Solution (100:1 Clearing Premix: Proteinase K) (Clearing Premix, Vizgen 20300003; Proteinase K, NEB P8107S) at 47 °C for 24 h.

For DAPI and PolyT staining, after removing the Clearing Solution, the sample was washed with a Sample Prep Wash Buffer. DAPI and PolyT Staining Reagent (Vizgen 20300021) were then added to the sample, which was incubated at room temperature for 15 min on a rocker. This was followed by a 10-min wash with Formamide Wash Buffer, then a 5 ml wash with 5 ml Sample Prep Buffer.

Finally, for MERFISH imaging, the sample was loaded onto the MERSCOPE instrument (MERSCOPE1.0, VIZGEN) for imaging, using the MERSCOPE 140 Gene Imaging Kit (Vizgen, 10400004), which automates the MERFISH probe exchange and readout.

To design an SC-specific MERFISH gene panel, we first assessed the number of genes required to classify SC neuron types. To this end, we implemented a simulation framework based on gradient boosting (XGBoost) using SC single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) data. In brief, for each neuron cluster, the top k non-redundant specific genes were selected to form a panel. The validation accuracy (using a 70:30 training:test split) was evaluated until a plateau was reached. Thus, after subsetting neuron cells from the adult SC snRNA-seq data28, we then re-clustered the cells using the Seurat standard log-normalization pipeline with the following functions: “NormalizeData” with default parameters, “FindVariableFeatures” (selection.method = ‘vst’), ScaleData (vars.to.regress =”nCount_RNA”), “RunPCA” (npcs=50), FindNeighbors (dims=1:35, dimension chosen by “ElbowPlot”), “FindClusters”, and “RunUMAP” (dim=35). The clusters were labelled based on the original cell-type labels, and 19 Leiden clusters recapitulating the original neuronal cell-type compartments were generated (Extended Data Fig. 2e). We then derived top marker genes for each type using the “FindAllMarkers” function with the “MAST” test (min.pct = 0.2, logfc.threshold=0.25, latent.vars = “nCount_RNA”).

To rank the marker genes, an integrated specificity score was calculated for each gene by retaining only those genes detected in over 40% of cells within the target cell type and calculating a log-ratio specificity score as:.

Industry observers note that where pct.1 and pct.2 represent the proportion of expressing cells in the target and background populations, respectively, and ϵ = 0.02 is a pseudocount. To integrate both specificity and fold change, z-scores were independently computed for the log-ratio specificity score and the average log2-transformed fold change (avg_log2FC) within each cluster. The final Stouffer score was computed as:.

The hybrid score captures both binary specificity (expression prevalence) and quantitative magnitude (fold change), enabling robust ranking of marker genes per cluster.

We next selected the top k (k = 1 to 10) non-redundant, high-specificity marker genes for each neuronal subtype (a total of 19 types, as identified above). We used them as features to train an XGBoost classifier. To ensure comparability across genes, the normalized expression matrix was subset to the selected gene panel and scaled by centreing each gene to its mean and dividing by its standard deviation (z-score normalization across cells). The classifier was trained using a multi-class softmax objective (multi:softprob) over 200 boosting rounds, with a learning rate (η) of 0.2, maximum tree depth of 6, and subsampling rate of 0.6 to mitigate overfitting. The number of output classes was set to the number of unique neuronal subtypes. Training was performed on 70% of the cells (stratified by cluster), and performance was evaluated on the 30% held-out data. For each cell, the predicted label corresponded to the class with the highest probability. A confusion matrix comparing predicted and true labels demonstrated high concordance, confirming that the MERFISH panel accurately recovered neuronal subtype heterogeneity. Classification accuracy as a function of gene panel size was summarized in a line plot (Extended Data Fig. 1e), revealing a performance plateau at 0.8414 when k = 9 (171 genes), followed by a slight decline to 0.8403 at k = 10 (190 genes). Notably, despite the inclusion of additional top marker genes, this accuracy remained lower than that achieved with the MERFISH gene panel (0.91).

It has been revealed that among the 140 genes included in the panel, we selected markers enriched in pan-excitatory, pan-inhibitory and type-specific neuronal populations. The 140 genes include Ntng1, Meis1, Cpne4, Cacna2d1, Sgcd, Spon1, Kctd8, Gpc5, Ptprk, Nxph1, Robo1, Hs3st4, Sorcs3, Chrm3, Mgat4c, Syt1, Car10, Pcbp3, Reln, Trpm3, Meis2, Prkd1, Epha3, Fras1, Il1rapl2, Tmem132d, Fstl4, Erbb4, Ebf3, Ebf1, Maf, Ptprt, Cdh18, Npas3Htr2c, Tfap2b, Etv1, Tshz2, Sorcs1, Lhfp, Col25a1, Sox6, Adarb2, Megf11, Pde1c, Csgalnact1, Cdh8, Chrm2, Tcf7l2, Sphkap, Arpp21, Kirrel3, Zfhx3, Tmem132c, Hcn1 Hdac9, Rorb, Pdzd2, Adam12, Ankfn1, Sntb1, Npnt, Gpc3, Kcnd3, Tpd52l1, Myh8, Cdh7, Barhl1, Kcnab1, Rd3l, Cbln4, Otx2, Gabrr2, Cdhr1, Sox14, Dmbx1, Lhx1os, Galnt14, Tnnt1, Tnni3, Fibcd1, Mgarp, Lmo1, Vwc2, Npffr1, Rnf152, Zfhx4, Tal1, Trim66, Gata3, Syt2, Nrtn, Smim17, Pax7, Cdh13, Slc17a6, Tac1, Cbln2, Kcng3, Kcng4, Cdh4, Pde5a, Gda, Foxp2, Pou4f2, Sema3e, Gad2, Npas4, Sdk2, Ppia, Atp5md, Mllt11, Calb2, Nap1l5, Gap43, Tacr1, C1ql2, Fabp5, Cxcl14, Stmn1, Fos, Snap25, Junb, Pmfbp1, Ntng2, Pcdh20, Satb1, Sv2c, Fign, Gfra1, Syt17, Rasgrf2, Lmo3, Slc19a1, Cplx3, Marcksl1, Cadps2, Calb1, Syt4 and Gad1.

Industry observers note that to further benchmark performance, we compared the 140-gene TransA-MERFISH panel against 2 control gene sets: (1) 140 genes randomly sampled from the full snRNA-seq expression matrix; and (2) 140 genes randomly sampled from the top 2,000 highly variable genes (HVGs). For each control set, we sampled genes without replacement and repeated the process 15 times to estimate variability (error bars) in classification accuracy. Using the same classification framework, our panel consistently outperformed both controls and the marker gene approach described above (Extended Data Fig. 1e). Two genes among the 140-gene panel (Sgcd and Ppia) were excluded due to low transcript detection in the TransA-MERFISH SC dataset and poor specificity for SC neuronal types.

Industry observers note that for each 12 µm tissue section, the MERFISH protocol generated seven 1.7 µm optical sections (z0, z1, … , z6) for DAPI, polyT and mCherry/RFP channels, respectively, as Tiff files under the images folder, together with the micron_to_mosaic_pixel_transform.csv to link the micrometre scale (transcripts and MERSCOPE visualizer) to mosaic pixel scale (Tiff files). Each MERFISH data folder also contains the detected_transcripts.csv file, which includes coordinates for detected transcripts along with their spatial coordinates, as well as other metadata and cell-by-gene information. Cell segmentation information is also generated by the Vizgen Post-processing Tool (VPT). To improve cell segmentation accuracy, we performed independent segmentation using custom scripts and a fine-tuned Cellpose2.0 model tailored to the SC, as described below.

The following steps were conducted: (1) DAPI image preprocessing and initial region-of-interest (ROI) selection. The DAPI image of z-plane 0 for each region is loaded into a Python Jupyter notebook (tifffile.imread), and overexposed pixels are filtered using a cut-off at the 0.95 quantile (np.quantile) to enhance the signal for downstream ROI selection. For each region, the initial ROI was restricted to the right SC hemisphere as our AAV2-mWmC injection was onto the left eye (Fig. 1a) and manually delineated using the processed DAPI image in ImageJ (Analyze-Tools-ROI manager), from the pial surface to encompass superficial SC layers (SZ and SGS) medially toward the midline, extending ventrally to the level of the cerebral aqueduct. This ROI includes both superficial and deeper layers as defined by cytoarchitectonic boundaries in the Allen Mouse Brain Atlas. We then cropped the original DAPI Tiff images of each seven z-plane images of one section to the delineated ROI (using the read_roi function, the matplotlib.patches module’s Polygon class, and the PIL package’s Image module). A maximum z-projection approach was performed over optical sections to enhance cell segmentation signals. To this end, the maximum-intensity projection of all seven z-plane optical sections for each slice was generated using either ImageJ (Images-Stack-Z Project) or Python (numpy.max). Meanwhile, we subset the detected_transcripts.csv file from MERFISH to correspond to the selected ROI (read-roi to load ImageJ ROI file, followed by matplotlib.path.Path in Python), using the micron_to_mosaic_pixel_transform.csv file to transform transcript coordinates (global_x and global_y coordinates) to the mosaic pixel coordinates of the Tiff images, along with gene symbols for each detected transcript.

Segmentation was performed as in previous MERFISH studies of the mouse brain31. We constructed a labelled image by combining the transcript dots and maximum-intensity projection DAPI images using the get_img function (windowsize=2000, margin=10%) of the ClusterMap package, followed by splitting the data into small tiles (split function) to improve downstream computational efficiency. We set a threshold of 3,000 transcript counts to focus on tiles with denser transcript accumulation. The split tiles were then saved as separate PNG files with DAPI signal and transcript dots overlaid. A customized Cellpose model66 (models.CellposeModel pretrained_model) was used to perform cell segmentation on each tile (gpu=True, channels = [0,0], diameter=80). More specifically, the fine-tuned Cellpose model was generated based on the ‘cyto2’ model using the Cellpose graphical user interface, trained with five regions of interest (containing about 200 manually curated cells each), to improve the performance for dimly/darkly stained cells, smaller cells, and separating multiple cells that were segmented as one. The segmentation output for each tile was subsequently generated using the masks_flows_to_seg function from cellpose.io and saved as a.npy file. The separate tiles were then stitched by merging adjacent patches, while avoiding cell ID collisions and duplication in overlapping regions, to form the full segmentation mask (reassigned_masks.npy), which encompassed the entire tissue section. After all tiles were stitched, connected components in the combined mask were relabelled (skimage.measure.label and regionprops) to ensure sequential, non-overlapping cell IDs. We then assembled the AnnData for downstream analysis by constructing a ClusterMap model for each section, using the transcriptomic spot information (xy_radius=30, z_radius=0, fast_preprocess=False). Centroid positions were calculated from labelled masks using skimage.regionprops, and used to initialize cell-centred AnnData objects. Cells with no transcriptomic counts were excluded by default, and spatial coordinates were stored in the obsm[‘spatial’] field of the AnnData object. We further double-checked the accuracy of the assembled AnnData by comparing the transcript distribution and the segmentation of a specific cell to the combined raw data for DAPI, PolyT, and transcript dots from the same cell in the MERSCOPE visualizer. We then integrated the mean mCherry fluorescence intensity, mWmC registration-related metadata, and the estimated depth (in µm; distance from the pial surface, as described below) into a unified AnnData object.

Recent findings suggest that last, related to the entire TransA-MERFISH data integration, for consistency with the ROI of other data modalities, such as electrophysiology and calcium imaging, we also further restricted the above-selected ROI to rectangular regions, avoiding the midlines and lateral regions, encompassing from the pial surface to SO by examining the spatial expression of Npnt and Etv1 (Fig. 1j). Subsequent clustering and transcriptomic analyses of the resulting cell-by-gene matrix were performed using Scanpy (v1.10.4) and Squidpy (v1.6.2), as detailed in the following sections.

To register mWmC+ cells in the TransA-MERFISH dataset, we implemented an automated registration workflow based on per-cell mCherry intensity, supplemented by manual curation. First, we derive the per-cell mean mCherry intensity by aggregating the mean mCherry pixel intensity at each z-layer (z = 1:6, excluding z0 to avoid potential optical noise). The aggregated value was then divided by the number of z-planes (six in this case, as the maximum-intensity projection-derived cell segmentation mask was shared across z-planes), yielding a per-cell mean mCherry intensity across z-planes. The frequency distribution of the per-cell mean mCherry intensity revealed a predominantly bimodal distribution of red fluorescence. Second, we assigned an mWmC-positive score using the mean intensity value from the inner cytoplasm ring area and an adjacent out-of-cell annulus as a local background estimate. The positive cells were identified by applying a threshold based on the distributions from a control ROI (in the lower, non-retino-recipient area with the lowest red fluorescence signal) on the same slice. Last, mWmC+ cells were proofread by two independent annotators for all slices, who examined the red fluorescence overlaid on the DAPI and PolyT labelling, with or without segmented cell masks, using Vizgen MERSCOPE Visualizer. The Python script for the workflow was deposited on GitHub (https://github.com/duanxlab/TransA-MERFISH).

For the background-corrected per-cell quantification of mCherry fluorescence, we implemented an integrated workflow for image denoising, fluorescence background removal, per-cell mWmC score calculation, and threshold assignment following the steps below.

First, background correction: to remove uneven illumination and background fluorescence (especially signals in axons, which reside in the same lamina as the recipient neurons), we applied a multi-threaded rolling-ball background subtraction algorithm to the RFP channel image. For each section, the maximum-intensity projection of z0–z7 optical planes was used as input. The image was processed in overlapping tiles (4,096 × 4,096 pixels) with a rolling-ball radius of 80 pixels. For each tile, the background surface was computed using the skimage.restoration.rolling_ball function, and the results were then merged across tiles to form a continuous background field. The corrected image was obtained by subtracting this field from the raw mosaic and clipping negative values to zero. The resulting background-subtracted image was used for downstream analyses. After this correction, the background intensity was reduced to baseline, thereby removing the haze surrounding individual cells. By contrast, the pixel intensity within cell masks is largely preserved. Second, further background removal and per-cell signal quantification: following the above background correction by rolling ball, residual local background (for example, neuropils and axons) around each labelled soma was estimated and removed using a ring-based subtraction procedure. In brief, for each segmented soma (cell i), the soma mask was eroded by 1 pixel to define a core region and then dilated by a 4-pixel guard band to prevent the background annulus from abutting the soma edge. This guarded soma was then surrounded by a series of concentric annuli (inner width = 8 pixels; outer radius range = 12–30 pixels) from which background intensity was sampled. Background pixels were sampled from the annulus after excluding any pixels belonging to other cells. The local background level Bi was defined as the 25th percentile of annular intensities. The corrected image \({I}^{{\prime} }(x,y)\) was computed as,.

For every soma and the designated ring configuration, we reported pre- and post-subtraction statistics within the inner measurement region (soma-adjacent ring):.

along with background noise estimates from the annulus:.

along with \({\sigma }_{\text{STD}}\) (sample standard deviation). After the removal of local background, the above-defined inner ring shows an improved local signal-to-noise ratio, and mWmC puncta signals stand out more.

It has been revealed that third, to define an internal control region and identify mWmC-positive cells in each section, we implemented automated identification of the control region and quantification of mWmC+ cells. In this pipeline, we used an automated depth-aware sliding-window analysis. For each cell i, the locally background-corrected fluorescence intensity was summarized by the mean pixel intensity within the soma’s inner measurement ring after local background subtraction, as described above. Cell centroids were computed from the segmentation mask, and a sliding window of height 800 µm was moved along the pial-to-deep axis in 100-µm increments. Within each window w, we computed the cumulative fluorescence energy as \({S}_{w}=\sum _{i\in w}{I}_{i},\) where Ii is the per-cell fluorescence metric (post-subtraction inner ring mean intensity in this case). Windows with fewer than 15 cells were excluded. The resulting curve Sw versus depth was smoothed with a seven-point moving average, and the valley (minimum) among valid windows was selected as the centre of the control region, corresponding to the zone of lowest cumulative signal (background). From this valley, the control region was symmetrically expanded until at least 600 cells were included. The final control region was exported as a rectangular ROI spanning the full mediolateral width. For all cells within the control ROI, Ii were aggregated to estimate the control population mean (μctrl) and standard deviation (σctrl). We then defined mWmC+ cells using the below threshold: after trimming the top 2% of brightest cells to exclude outliers confounded by, for example, neighbouring overexposed pixels, thresholds for positive detection were defined as T5σ = μctrl + 5σctrl as the baseline to register mWmC+ cells.

Finally, with the per-cell mWmC information, we further assigned a cell type as mWmC+ (retino-recipient) by first deriving the mWmC+ cell profiles across different cell types using the methods described above. Encouragingly, automatically assigned mWmC+ cell profiles correlate strongly with manual annotations, indicating consistency across methods. To quantify enrichment of mWmC+ cells across neuronal subtypes, we computed an enrichment score for each tracing and cell type using the following steps. For each tracing × cell type, we constructed a 2 × 2 table of mWmC+ and mWmC− counts inside the cell type versus all other cells and applied a one-tailed Fisher’s exact test (alternative = “greater”). The odds ratio (OR) was computed as:.

Sources indicate that where a and b are the numbers of mWmC+ and mWmC− cells within the given subtype, and c and d are the corresponding counts outside that subtype. The effect size was visualized as log2(OR) (values < 0 clipped to 0). At the same time, statistical evidence was encoded by a point area proportional to −log10(P). Cell types with positive enrichment (log2(OR) > 0) were highlighted with a red outline (Fig. 2o). We assign a cell type as positive or connected under a specific tracing condition when the log2(OR) value is greater than 0 (enrichment). Based on the mWmC+ cell types assigned here, we summarized the mean mWmC+ cell proportion across animals (error bar: s.e.m.) as bar plots (Figs. 1k and 3c).

Recent findings suggest that the neuronal subset was re-clustered using a similar framework as described above. To determine parameters better reflect internal data structure and cell-type granularity, we chose clustering parameters based on statistical assessment and established parameter selection tools. Principal component dimensionality (n_pcs = 12) was selected based on inspection of the variance explained curve (sc.pl.pca_variance_ratio). Clustering resolution was subsequently determined using the clustering tree approach implemented in the clustree R package to assess cluster stability across multiple resolutions, and a resolution of 1.5 was selected. The parameter selections here allowed us to settle on a granularity of cell types that best represent the internal data structure in an unbiased way. These clusters were then labelled using the approaches described below. Subsequent comparisons to published SC atlas indicated high consistency, for example, when compared to the 10x Whole Mouse Brain Atlas at supertype level, supporting the robustness of selected parameters and the resulting granularity of cell types.

To perform clustering and dimension reduction, we first applied SCTransform-based normalization67 to the expression matrix for each MERFISH section. This was enabled by accessing the SCTransform algorithm implemented in the R package via rpy2 from Python. Prior to normalization, raw counts were stored in adata.layers[‘raw_counts’]. A quality control filtering step was then applied to remove low-quality features, retaining genes detected in at least 5 cells (sc.pp.filter_genes) and cells with a total count of at least 5 (sc.pp.filter_cells). After filtering, the sparse matrices were explicitly sorted to ensure compatibility. Each AnnData object was converted to a Seurat object (as.Seurat()), and SCTransform was applied (do.correct.umi = FALSE). SCTransform models sequencing depth (library size/total unique molecular identifiers (UMIs)) as a technical covariate during normalization. The full set of normalized gene expression values was extracted from the SCT assay’s scale.data slot and stored in adata.layers[‘normalized’], ensuring that any genes missing post-normalization were reintroduced as zero-filled vectors to retain consistency with the original feature set. The normalized matrix was then assigned to adata.X for downstream analysis. Raw counts were preserved in adata.raw, and standard quality control metrics (n_genes_by_counts, total_counts) were computed using the raw layer. Based on the quality control metrics, two sections with low quality and significantly lower counts were excluded from further analysis.

Recent findings suggest that the AnnDatas of the remaining MERFISH slices were subsequently merged using scanpy (v1.10.4; abbreviated as sc onwards) with ad.concat (merge = ‘unique’, index_unique=None), yielding a combined dataset of 47,740 cells. Cell identifiers were made unique across slices, and principal component analysis was performed on the merged expression matrix (sc.tl.pca). The variance explained by each component was examined to guide dimensionality reduction (sc.pl.pca_variance_ratio). A neighbourhood graph was constructed using the top 15 principal components (n_pcs = 15) and 30 nearest neighbours (n_neighbors = 30) by sc.pp.neighbors. UMAP was then applied for two-dimensional embedding (sc.tl.umap). Unsupervised clustering was carried out using the Leiden algorithm with a resolution parameter of 0.8 (sc.tl.leiden). We examined the distribution of quality control metrics across the clusters. We found high consistency of n_genes_by_counts and total_counts across clusters except lower detection rate in one cluster (Extended Data Fig. 1h), which was identified as non-neuronal cells via the SC XGBoost classifier as described above (Extended Data Fig. 1i). To improve classification resolution, the non-neuronal cluster was excluded, yielding 46,277 high-quality transcriptomic profiles for neuronal cells. The neuronal subset was re-clustered using a similar framework as described above. Principal component dimensionality (n_pcs = 12) was selected based on inspection of the variance explained curve (sc.pl.pca_variance_ratio). Clustering resolution was subsequently determined using the clustering tree approach implemented in the clustree R package to assess cluster stability across multiple resolutions, and a resolution of 1.5 was selected. These clusters were then labelled using the approaches described below.

Sources indicate that to robustly identify the molecular identity of the above-identified MERFISH clusters, we took the following steps to classify the identified clusters and compare them to established SC atlases: first, we examined the gene expression pattern for a set of SC canonical marker genes (Fig. 1g) and the dendrogram between these clusters based on hierarchical clustering of averaged expression per cluster (sc.tl.dendrogram). Second, we aligned our MERFISH data to the 10x Whole Mouse Brain (CCN20230722) taxonomy30 using the MapMyCells tool suite from the Allen Institute. Third, we utilized the XGBoost classifier, as described above, to link the MERFISH data to our and other published SC scRNA-seq or snRNA-seq neuron-type atlases6,27,28, using the shared genes between the MERFISH panel and the snRNA-seq genes as features (Extended Data Fig. 2c,g,j). Finally, we compared the expression pattern of key marker genes between our data and previously published SC datasets (Extended Data Fig. 2d). Overall, the identified clusters captured the neuronal diversity of the SC at high resolution, demonstrating strong concordance—and in some cases, enhanced granularity—compared to established reference atlases.

It has been revealed that we implemented a sublaminar-controlled cell-type specificity analysis to test the specificity of each SC type in specifying the connections with presynaptic RGC inputs (Fig. 2d). The analysis is based on a permutation-based statistical framework with Stouffer z-score aggregation across mice. More specifically, to assess cell-type–specific enrichment or depletion of mWmC+ labelling independent of sublaminar distribution, we performed a sublaminar-controlled permutation test. Within each mouse, SC neurons were binned by soma depth (50 µm unless otherwise specified). Within each (animal × depth bin) stratum, cell-type labels were randomly shuffled, thereby preserving the sublaminar distribution of mWmC labelling while disrupting the association between cell-type identity and mWmC labelling. All permutation tests were performed with 1,000 permutations using a fixed random seed unless otherwise stated. For each permutation, we computed the number of mWmC+ cells per cell type, yielding a null distribution of expected counts under the hypothesis that sublaminar position alone explains connectivity. Observed mWmC+ cell counts were then converted into per-animal z-scores relative to this null distribution. Specifically, for each cell type t and mouse q, the z-score was computed as follows,.

According to recent reports, where \({N}_{t,q}^{\mathrm{obs}}\) denotes the observed number of mWmC+ cells of type t in mouse q, and μt,q and σt,q denote the mean and standard deviation of the permutation-derived null distribution for that cell type and mouse. z-Scores provide a signed, normalized measure of enrichment or depletion relative to sublaminar expectation. z-Scores were then aggregated across mice using Stouffer’s method as below,.

where n is the number of mice. To test for bidirectional deviations (enrichment or depletion) of mWmC labelling beyond sublaminar expectation, two-sided P values were computed from the combined z-scores using the standard normal distribution as,.

and controlled for multiple comparisons across cell types using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate procedure. Positive z-scores indicate enrichment beyond sublaminar expectation, whereas negative z-scores indicate depletion, reflecting cases in which sublaminar position alone overestimates the likelihood of receiving retinal input. As statistical inference is performed using normal-theory P values derived from the aggregated z-scores (after estimating null mean and variance from permutations), the minimum attainable P value is not constrained by the number of permutations. Finally, SC neuron types were ranked by their aggregated Stouffer z-scores, which we refer to as the cell-type specificity score, representing the preference of a cell type’s molecular identity for RGC connectivity (Fig. 2e).

RGC axons in the SC from four different genotypes and all RGCs were included. In brief, coronal brain sections were immunostained and imaged using a confocal microscope, as previously described43. Confocal stacks of 20 µm thickness were acquired and processed to generate maximum-intensity projections. Using ImageJ, each right SC hemisphere was divided into five equal sections. The fluorescence profile of axon arbors was measured by taking 200-μm-thick line scans perpendicular to each section’s pial surface, extending to a depth of 500 μm below it. Signal intensity values were normalized to the maximum intensity across images and plotted. The locally weighted scatterplot smoothing function in MATLAB was used to smooth the curve. ImageJ was used to analyse confocal stacks and produce maximum-intensity projections. To quantify axon depth across the SC, the shortest distance from the pial surface to the upper and lower boundaries of the axonal arbors was measured within each section. Five mice of each genotype, including all SC slices, were used for each experimental condition. For experiments in which multiple neurons were recorded from the same mouse, mouse identity was treated as the experimental unit/random effect to account for the hierarchical structure of the data.

The retina histology protocol was described as previously described50. Mice were euthanized, and eyes were collected, then fixed in 4% PFA/PBS for 1 h on ice. Retinas were dissected and rinsed with PBS. For the whole-mount retina data in Fig. 3, we adapted previously described protocols37. Whole-mount retina samples were blocked in blocking buffer (5% normal donkey serum, 0.5% Triton X-100 in PBS) at room temperature for 1 h, then incubated with primary antibodies for 2–4 days at 4 °C, followed by secondary antibodies for 2 h at room temperature. For mounting, retinas were placed flat, ganglion cell side up, and sealed with Fluoromount-G (SouthernBiotech, 0100-01). For retinal vertical sections in Extended Data Fig. 6, we adapted protocols previously described37. Fixed mouse retinas were cryoprotected in 30% sucrose in PBS for 1 h before embedding in OCT (Epredia). Vertical retinal cryosections (20 µm) were prepared and mounted on glass slides. Sections were blocked in the same blocking buffer and incubated with primary antibodies overnight at 4 °C, followed by secondary antibodies for 1 h at room temperature. Sections were sealed with Fluoromount-G (SouthernBiotech) containing DAPI.

Brain section histology was described previously68. Mice were deeply anaesthetized and perfused transcardially with ice-cold PBS, followed by 4% PFA. Brains were post-fixed in 4% PFA overnight at 4 °C, then cryoprotected in 30% sucrose in PBS at 4 °C until the tissue blocks sank. Tissue was frozen directly on the stage of a sliding microtome (Leica) cooled with dry ice and sectioned coronally at 40 µm. Free-floating sections were blocked in the blocking buffer described above and incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies, then for 1 h at room temperature with secondary antibodies. Sections were mounted on slides with Fluoromount-G (SouthernBiotech) containing DAPI.

Antibodies used were as follows: goat and chicken anti-GFP (1:1,000, Rockland; 1:500, Abcam); rabbit anti-RFP (1:1,000, Rockland for immunohistochemistry); mouse anti-SATB1 (marker for ooDSGC in reference69, 1:1,000, Santa Cruz); goat anti-choline acetyltransferase (ChAT, 1:500, Millipore); rabbit anti-CARTPT (1:2,500, Phoenix Pharmaceuticals); rabbit anti-TUSC5 (1:500, Novus); Rabbit anti-RBPMS (1:1,000, Poteintech/Fisher); goat anti-SPP1 (1:500, R&D); sheep anti-FOXP2 (1:500, R&D); rabbit anti-ETV1 (1:1,000, J.A.K.)70. Secondary antibodies were conjugated to Alexa Fluor 488, Alexa Fluor 568, or Alexa Fluor 647 (Jackson ImmunoResearch) and used at 1:1,000.

It has been revealed that in situ hybridization was performed as previously described68 using RNAscope Fluorescent Multiplex Kit (Advanced Cell Diagnostics) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. In brief, sections were fixed in 4% PFA and dehydrated as described in ‘Immunohistochemistry for the retina and SC’, followed by air drying. A hydrophobic barrier was drawn around the sections with an ImmEdge pen (Vector Labs, H-4000). The sections were post-fixed with 4% PFA, quenched with hydrogen peroxide, and subjected to target retrieval followed by dehydration in 100% ethanol. Sections were treated with Protease III, incubated with target probes, treated with a series of amplification reagents, and developed with TSA fluorophores. Slides were mounted using mounting medium (VECTASHIELD, Vector Laboratories). RNAscope probes included the following: Cdh7 (ACD #521331), Cbln4 (ACD #505411), Itga7 (ACD #542911) and Sntb1 (ACD #440541).

It has been revealed that intraocular injection of AAVs was performed as previously described37,41. Approximately 0.5 µl of virus was delivered into the left eye using a sharpened glass micropipette. All AAVs (serotype 2 targeting RGCs) were standardized to the same titre of 2 × 1013 genome copies. Mice were euthanized, and retinas and brains were collected about 4 weeks post-injection (wpi).

For mWmC-based anterograde tracing experiments, AAV encoding constitutive mWmC or Cre-dependent mWmC was intravitreally injected into wild-type, Kcng4-cre, Cartpt-cre, Foxp2-cre and Tusc5-cre mice. AAVs were injected into the left eyes using a sharpened glass pipette as previously described19. Mice were processed for analysis at 4 wpi.

For optogenetic experiments, AAV2-CAG-ChR2-mCherry-WPRE, AAV2-EF1α-DIO-ChR2(H134R)-EYFP, AAV2-EF1α-DIO-ChR2(H134R)-mCherry were injected into the left eyes of mice to activate all RGCs or ooDSGCs. Mice were allowed to mature for at least 6 wpi, reaching adulthood (6–10 weeks) before analysis.

Recent findings suggest that for starburst amacrine cell (Chat+) ablation experiments, AAV2-Flex-taCasp3-TEVp was injected into the left eye or both eyes of mice in the ablation groups. 2 sites located at the dorsal and ventral parts of the eyeball were used for injection; 0.75 µl of virus was injected into each site. For the control groups, same volume of saline was injected into the left eye of mice. Two-photon calcium imaging was performed 1 month after injection.

In a recent development, for adult SC labelling, mice were anaesthetized with isoflurane during the surgery (3% for induction and 1.5–2% for maintenance) and placed in a stereotaxic apparatus (Model 940, David Kopf Instruments). Meloxicam (5 mg kg−1) was administered intraperitoneally for analgesia before the surgery and 1 day after the surgery. Body temperature was maintained at 37 °C using a homeothermic blanket. Viral solutions were loaded into a pulled glass pipette connected to a syringe (7634-0, Hamilton) via a dual-ferrule adaptor (55750-0, Hamilton). The injection speed and volume were controlled by a Microinjection Syringe Pump (UMP3T-1, WPI). AAV2-EF1a-FDIO-mCherry or AAV2-EF1a-FDIO-EGFP (1 µl) was injected into the right SC of adult mice at a constant speed (60 nl min−1).

Two injection sites were used for the Cdh7-FlpO and Cbln4-FlpO lines: one at 0.35 mm posterior and 0.5 mm lateral to lambda at a depth of 1.3 mm, and the other at 0.1 mm posterior and 0.6 mm lateral to lambda at a depth of 1.2 mm. The mice were transcardially perfused at 4 wpi. The brains were collected for immunohistochemical analysis. In addition, specifically for pseudorabies-mediated retrograde tracing, AAV8-hSyn-FRT-TVA-P2A-EGFP-2A-oG viruses (1 µl) were injected into the right SC of the Cdh7-FlpO or Cbln4-FlpO adult mice by stereotaxic injections as described above. Three weeks later, EnvA G-Deleted Rabies-mCherry (1.2 µl) was injected into the right SC. Six days post-rabies injection, mice were transcardially perfused, and brains and contralateral (left) retinas were collected for immunohistochemical analysis.

We used the Cre/FlpO strategy to label SC neurons and manipulate RGCs separately by crossing RGC-specific Cre drivers to SC-specific FlpO mice. After injecting AAV2-EF1α-FDIO-GFP-WPRE into the right SC of Cbln4-FlpO or Cdh7-FlpO mice, we can target recording from GFP-labelled SC neurons. By injecting AAV2-CAG-ChR2-mCherry-WPRE to manipulate all RGCs or AAV2-EF1α-DIO-ChR2(H134R)-mCherry to manipulate specific types of RGCs into the left eye, a blue light (473 nm, 15 mW mm−2) can activate the RGC axon terminals in the SC.

Injected mice were anaesthetized by ketamine and xylazine (100 mg kg−1, 12.5 mg kg−1) and transcardially perfused with ice-cold Cutting solution (78.3 mM NaCl, 2.3 mM KCl, 33.8 mM choline-Cl, 0.45 mM CaCl2, 6.4 mM MgCl2, 1.1 mM NaH2PO4, 23 mM NaHCO3, 20 mM D-glucose, 0.5 mM L-glutamine, pH 7.4). The brains were dissected, and coronal brain sections were prepared using a vibratome (VT1200S, Leica) in ice-cold, carbogenated Cutting solution. Slices (250 μm in thickness) with SC were collected and transferred to a 32.5 °C incubation chamber filled with carbogenated Cutting solution. After 30 min incubation, the slices were transferred to room temperature artificial cerebrospinal fluid (ACSF; 125 mM NaCl, 2.5 mM KCl, 1.25 mM NaH2PO4, 26 mM NaHCO3, 1 mM MgCl2·6H2O, 2 mM CaCl2, 20 mM D-glucose, pH 7.4) before recording. Cutting solutions and ACSF were constantly bubbled with 5% CO2 and 95% O2 (Carbogen, Airgas).

Sources indicate that A CCD camera (IR-2000, DAGE-MTI) mounted on a fluorescence microscope (BX51WI, Olympus) was used to detect a green cell surrounded by red axon terminals. Targeted whole-cell recordings were made under IR-DIC visualization. The glass pipettes (BF150-86-10, Sutter Instrument) were pulled by a puller (P1000, Sutter Instrument) into recording electrodes (3–5 MΩ). The recording electrode was filled with potassium-based internal solutions (135 mM potassium gluconate, 8 mM KCl, 10 mM HEPES, 0.25 mM EGTA, 2 mM MgATP, 0.3 mM Na2GTP, 7 mM phosphocreatine, pH 7.3). All data were acquired using a MultiClamp 700B Amplifier and a 1440A DigiData (Molecular Devices). The signals were digitized at 10 kHz and low-pass filtered at 1 kHz. Axon activation was performed using a 473 nm LED (Cool LED, pE300). Five light pulses (2 ms) were delivered per trial. After breaking into the cells, we held them at −65 mV and applied whole-cell compensation. Voltage-clamp mode was used to record evoked EPSCs, and current-clamp mode was used to record action potentials. Tetrodotoxin (TTX, 1 µM) and 4-aminopyridine (4-AP, 100 µM) were added to ACSF perfusions to confirm the monosynaptic connection. CNQX (10 µM) and APV (50 µM) were added to confirm the glutamatergic synapses. For experiments in which multiple neurons were recorded from the same mouse, mouse identity was treated as the experimental unit or random effect to account for the hierarchical structure of the data.

Sources indicate that an internal solution containing Biocytin (0.5%, B4261-100mg, Sigma) was used for electrophysiological recording and dye filling, as previously described71. After recording, brain slices were fixed with 4% PFA overnight at 4 °C, then blocked with blocking solution (PBS with 0.3% TritonX-100 and 5% normal donkey serum) for one day at 4 °C. Then the slices were incubated with Streptavidin-488 or 555 (1:1,000, Invitrogen) for 2 h at room temperature. After mounting the slices, the images were acquired by a Zeiss confocal microscope (LSM900).

In vivo calcium imaging of mouse SC was performed using a two-photon microscope as previously described72.

Surgeries were performed on eight-week-old transgenic mice. The craniotomy, virus injection, and transparent silicone plug insertion were done over the right SC. Mice were anaesthetized with ketamine and xylazine and placed in a stereotaxic device with their eyes covered with ophthalmic ointment. Mice were anaesthetized with 2% isoflurane for maintenance and injected with meloxicam (5 mg kg−1). Craniotomy was performed over the lambda of the skull, and a large flap was opened in the dura with a forceps (Dumoxel-Biology 11252-30, FST). We injected the right SC with 400 nl of AAV8-EF1α-FDIO-GCaMP6s. A silicone plug bonded to a 5 mm circular coverslip was mounted on a suction cup and positioned over the craniotomy. The plug advanced downward to press the brain and then anteriorly to displace the dura and transverse sinuses. A drop of cyanoacrylate (Vetbond, 3 M) was used to fix the silicon plug to the skull, then the suction was released, and the suction cup was withdrawn. A custom head plate (titanium, 1 mm thick, eMachineShop) was bonded to the skull by cyanoacrylate (Vetbond, 3 M) and dental cement (Ortho-Jet, LangDental). At least 2 weeks after implanting cranial windows, mice were habituated to handling and head-fixing at least 4 times under a two-photon microscope.

Recent findings suggest that we imaged calcium responses in mice using a two-photon microscope (Neurolabware) with a Spectra-Physics MaiTai laser at 920 nm (15–50 mW) to excite GCaMP6s. Imaging in the SC was performed at depths of 50–200 µm below the pia surface. A 575 × 370 µm field of view was scanned at 15.5 Hz, producing a series of 416 × 268-pixel images. A tangent LCD screen (Dell, U2312HM) placed in front of the left eye of head-fixed mice will present a visual stimulus generated with Psychtoolbox3 (MATLAB) and synchronized with image acquisition via TTL signals from the stimulus screen. The screen is centred 14 cm away from the mouse, angled at 20 degrees in pitch and yaw to minimize fisheye distortion. We imaged each mouse for about 1 h, with multiple sessions on successive days if needed to present a battery of visual stimuli and acquire stable imaging.

Visual stimuli were presented on a tangent (1,920 × 1,080 pixels) region of the screen. The screen was strobed for 2 µs at the end of each scan line (1,200 Hz; luminance of the grey screen, 1.25 cd m−2; maximum brightness, 1/80 of the unmodified monitor) to minimize interference between the visual stimulus and two-photon fluorescence detection. All stimuli presented used only the green and blue channels of the screen. Red bars flickered periodically at the bottom of the screen, which was covered with black tape, to convey the timing of the visual stimulus to synchronize with fluorescence acquisition. All visual stimuli in two-photon experiments were presented in a pseudorandom sequence, interspersed with blank periods within each stimulus block, using a different random seed for each block. Moving gratings were used to test the direction selectivity of SC neurons. The drifting grating was 100 pixels wide (6.4°), with black or white bars, and drifted in 8 directions (45° intervals) at a speed of 356 pixels per second (22.7° per second). To map receptive fields, flashing spots were presented in a 9 × 5 position arrayed across the stimulus monitor. Each spot was a 216 × 216 pixel (13.8° × 13.8°) square that appeared for 1 second. All visual stimuli were repeated six times per trial.

It has been revealed that to test the contribution of the ipsilateral eye to the direction selectivity of Cbln4+ SC neurons, we covered the ipsilateral eye with a black box during calcium imaging. The box was removed after the experiments.

We performed offline motion correction of calcium imaging data by NoRMCorre73, identified GCaMP6s+ cells, extracted calcium traces for each cell, and subtracted neuropil signals. Next, we aligned traces to visual stimuli using synchronization pulses relayed from stimulus monitors to the microscope via a TTL signal, which were time-stamped in the imaging data. For traces with high-peak noisy spikes (large mouse motion that cannot be corrected), we used a denoising algorithm to replace noisy dots with smooth traces. The noisy spike traces were determined by whether any points were bigger than the mean ± 4 s.d. traces. Then, calcium traces were aligned to the onset of each visual stimulus, averaged across trials, and the peak and valley of each mean trace were identified.

It has been revealed that DSI calculation followed a previously published protocol74. ΔF/F values for each presentation of a stimulus were averaged from six repeats, and the peak ΔF/F for each direction was used to compute direction preference. The direction selectivity index (DSI) was calculated as the normalized amplitude of the vector sum of all directions by their scalar sum. Cells with DSI > 0.2 were classified as direction selective. The preferred direction was defined as the weighted vector sum over eight stimulus angles.

For confocal image acquisition, all procedures were conducted in a double-blind manner. One researcher collected images without knowledge of genotype, while a second researcher, who performed the analysis, was also blinded. Littermates were used as controls in all experiments unless otherwise indicated. Both male and female mice were included. Images were acquired on a Zeiss LSM900 confocal microscope (Carl Zeiss Microscopy) equipped with 10× air, 20× air and 40× oil immersion objectives.

Sources indicate that to quantify immunostained cells in the SC and retina, confocal images of vertical retinal sections, coronal SC sections, and whole-mount retina were collected under identical imaging conditions across all samples. Confocal stacks of 20 µm (retina and SC sections) or 60 µm (whole-mount retina) were acquired and processed to generate maximum-intensity projections. Cells positive for each marker was identified using thresholded fluorescence intensity criteria. Single-positive and double-positive cells were manually counted with the Cell Counter plugin in ImageJ (NIH). For RNAscope in situ hybridization, SC sections processed with RNAscope and immunostaining were imaged on a Zeiss LSM900 with a 20× objective. The number of GFP-positive neurons or marker-positive cells was counted across all stained samples as mentioned above. Data were pooled across animals, and results are presented as percentages (mean ± s.e.m.). Confocal image files for histology were analysed using Fiji Image J (v1.53c), Microsoft Excel 365, Graph Pad Prism9, Adobe Illustrator 2020. Electrophysiological data collection and analysis were not performed blindly with respect to the experimental conditions. All whole-cell recording data were acquired by Camplex 10.7 (Molecular Devices) and analysed in MATLAB (MathWorks) or Clampfit 10.7 (Molecular Devices). Optogenetically evoked currents were averaged across 5 trials. Clampfit 10.7 measured the peak amplitudes of evoked currents. MATLAB analysed the intrinsic properties of recorded neurons. All statistics were calculated by GraphPad Prism 9. Peak currents between the two groups were compared using a two-tailed Student’s t-test.

Optomotor response was described previously75. The OptoDrum (Striatech) comprises a box with four screens to simulate drifting gratings. An IR camera mounted on the top of the box was used to record mouse movements. Mice were first acclimated to the room in their cages for 30 min. Then, freely moving mice were placed on a platform and allowed to acclimate to the box for at least 5 min. Drifting gratings (12° s−1) in the clockwise direction can trigger left-eye-mediated body and head movements, while drifting gratings in the counterclockwise direction were used to test right-eye-mediated movements. Drifting gratings were presented from low spatial frequencies (0.056 cycles per degree) to high frequencies (0.3–0.5 cycles per degree) to determine the threshold at which a mouse could track. OptoDrum’s software can detect the body shape of mice and label the positions of head, body, and tail of mice. The stimulus and video tracking were paused if a mouse engaged in grooming behaviour or dropped off the platform and resumed later. The software can score the optomotor response and determine the spatial-frequency threshold. False positives were manually identified as invalid, and the same frequency of drifting gratings was repeated. We compared the spatial-frequency threshold of drifting gratings to trigger optomotor responses in the left eye (ablation) with the right eye (control) to assess visual acuity differences.

According to recent reports, we obtained measurements from distinct biological samples. No covariates were tested. No formal test of normality was performed; statistical tests were selected based on the distributional assumptions of the data. Statistical methods and the number of animals tested for each configuration are documented in the figure legends for each experiment. When comparing two groups, statistics were derived using an unpaired two-sided Student’s t-test, Kolmogorov–Smirnov test or Fisher’s exact test, as indicated in the figure legends. For comparing cell-type proportions across multiple reactions, we used the Kruskal–Wallis H test (scipy.stats.kruskal, Python). One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed in GraphPad Prism 9 to assess the statistical significance of differences among multiple measurements.

Fisher’s exact test was performed using the Easy Fisher Exact Test Calculator (https://www.socscistatistics.com/tests/fisher/default2.aspx).

Statistical significance was defined as *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001 and ****P < 0.0001. All values indicate mean ± s.e.m., unless otherwise noted.

a, Unsupervised classification of sSC using the standard fresh-frozen MERFISH protocol. UMAP embedding of 5,845 cells reveals consistent clustering of the same 8 ENCs and 11 INCs identified with TransA-MERFISH on fixed tissue (Fig. 1d). Cell-type labels were assigned to Leiden clusters based on canonical marker gene expression patterns and transcriptomic mapping via a supervised XGBoost classifier trained on the TransA-MERFISH atlas. b, Confusion matrix showing transcriptomic correspondence between cell types in standard MERFISH (rows) and TransA-MERFISH (columns). c, Violin plots comparing quality control metrics between standard MERFISH (blue) and TransA-MERFISH (gray). Distributions are highly similar across key metrics, including the number of genes detected per cell (n_genes_by_counts), total transcript counts per cell (total_counts), and cell mask area (in pixels). A modest reduction in n_genes_by_counts and total_counts was observed in TransA-MERFISH experiments. d, Comparison of matched neuronal subtype frequencies between standard MERFISH and TransA-MERFISH. Values are plotted on a ln-ln scale to highlight low-frequency types. A strong correlation is observed across both excitatory and inhibitory populations, indicating that the TransA-MERFISH protocol did not bias or deplete neuron types in the sSC (Pearson R = 0.88). e, Validation accuracies of the XGBoost classifier trained using various gene selection strategies: the performance of the 140-gene TransA-MERFISH panel was compared to randomly sampled 140-gene sets drawn from either the full single-cell transcriptome or the top 2000 highly variable genes (HVGs). Additional gene sets were constructed by selecting the top k specific genes (Methods) per SC neuronal cluster (k = 1–10), based on 19 neuronal clusters identified from re-clustering of the neuronal subset of the dataset28. Data are presented as mean ± SD. f, Dot plots comparing the expression patterns of 2 non-optimal probes (top row, blue) with their corresponding expressions in snRNA-seq17 (bottom row, orange). MERFISH cells are grouped according to their predicted snRNA-seq cluster identities, as inferred by Tangram-based imputation (Methods). The 140-gene list is presented in Supplementary Table 1. g-j, Classification and filtering of non-neuron cells (NNs). UMAP embedding (g) of all high-quality cells (47740 cells after quality filtering, see Methods) before filtering out non-neuronal cells, colored by broad cell classes: excitatory neurons (ENCs), inhibitory neurons (INCs), and NNs. NNs were identified using a supervised XGBoost classifier (i) trained on an SC snRNA-seq dataset, as in the reference28. Violin plots (h) of quality control metrics show that NNs exhibit reduced numbers of detected genes per cell (n_genes_by_counts) and total transcripts per cell (total_counts), consistent with the design principles for neurons in the TransA-MERFISH gene panel. Bar plots (j) showing the average proportions of ENCs and INCs among all detected cells across animals. NNs were subsequently filtered out before re-clustering of neuronal cells to improve classification resolution among neuronal types. n = 16 animals. Data are presented as mean ± s.e.m.

Sources indicate that a,b, Transcriptomic correspondence between the MERFISH-based sSC neuron atlas and the 10x Genomics-based Whole Mouse Brain (WMB) taxonomy (CCN20230722; Allen Institute)20. (a) UMAP embedding of the TransA-MERFISH neuron atlas (Fig. 1d), colored by the most probable mapped supertype identity inferred via MapMyCells. (b) Confusion matrix showing the correspondence between TransA-MERFISH neuronal types (rows) and 10 x WMB supertypes (columns), as determined by MapMyCells mapping (Methods). c, Transcriptomic correspondence between the TransA-MERFISH sSC neuron atlas and the Trans-Seq single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) SC neuron atlas9, as determined by XGBoost-based classification (Methods). Dot size and color represent the proportion of cells from each Trans-Seq cluster (y-axis) mapped to the corresponding TransA-MERFISH neuronal types (x-axis), indicating the scRNA-seq-based protocol biases a few neuronal subsets due to the nature of the dissociation and FACS sorting, thus it is not optimal to represent adult neuron clusters precisely and comprehensively. d, Dot plot comparing transcriptomic signatures of representative neuronal types across three datasets: TransA-MERFISH (red), single-nucleus RNA-seq (green)22, and supertypes from the 10x Genomics-based Whole Mouse Brain (WMB) taxonomy (blue; corresponding to panels a,b). Shown are selected excitatory neuron types—including Cdh7+ SC neurons (ENC1, ENC2), Npnt+ wide-field SC neurons (ENC5), and Etv1+ SC neurons (ENC6)—as well as inhibitory neuron types, including Cbln4+ SC neurons (INC1) and Fibcd1+ SC neurons (INC3). The consistent expression patterns of key marker genes across datasets support the robustness of cell classification in the TransA-MERFISH atlas and align with mapping results obtained via machine learning (g,j) and MapMyCells (a,b). e-j, Alignments of the TransA-MERFISH neuronal clusters with past single-nucleus RNA-seq (snRNA-Seq) atlases of the mouse SC, indicating consistency across datasets. Re-clustering of neuronal subsets from reference datasets reproduced the original cell-type assignments (e17 and h22). Confusion matrices (f,i) show that XGBoost models trained on the 140-gene TransA-MERFISH panel achieve high validation accuracy in recovering snRNA-seq-defined cell types. Heatmaps (g,j) show the transcriptomic correspondence between snRNA-seq cell clusters (y-axis) and the TransA-MERFISH types (x-axis), based on predictions from an XGBoost classifier trained on the TransA-MERFISH dataset using the 140 genes. Color intensity reflects the percentage of cells from each snRNA-seq cluster mapped to each TransA-MERFISH type.

a-b, UMAP embedding of TransA-MERFISH neuron atlas (Fig. 1d), with cells colored by individual dataset identities corresponding to each reaction (a), and split UMAP embedding for each replicate separately (b), showing consistent cluster structure across replicates. c, Histograms display consistent percentages of neurons for each dataset contributing to each identified neuron type, for a stable representation of cell types across datasets. d, Violin plots showing the distributions of the number of genes detected per cell (n_genes_by_counts) and total transcripts detected per cell (total counts) across each of the 19 sSC neuronal types. Data are presented as mean ± s.e.m. f, UMAP embedding of TransA-MERFISH neuron atlas (Fig. 1d), with mWmC+ neurons colored by individual dataset identities corresponding to each reaction (as in panel a). g, UMAP distribution for each of the three datasets separately, showing that all mWmC+ types have contributions from three reactions. e, Stacked barplot demonstrates consistent mWmC+ labeling of each retino-recipient neuron type across datasets, ensuring a stable representation of retino-recipient cell types. h, Bar plots showing the proportions of each cell type across the three replicates. Comparisons across tracing conditions using the Kruskal–Wallis test revealed no differences among cell types (p > 0.05). Data are presented as mean ± SD. i, left, Example of raw MERFISH images with DAPI (gray) and RNA transcripts (blue); colored segmented cell masks are generated using a customized Cellpose 2.0 model. middle, Similar to (left) but overlapped with curated colored masks annotated manually as a benchmark. right, Comparison of Cellpose model-generated masks and curated masks. Light green shows true positive (TP), pink show False Positive (FP), and purple show False Negative (FN). j, Violin plot showing the performance score across three animals. Calculation of precision, recall and F1 are as following: Precision = TP / (TP + FP), Recall = TP / (TP + FN), F1 = 2 * Precision * Recall / (Precision + Recall). The horizontal line within the violin indicates the median. k, Violin plot showing the distribution of Intersection over Union (IoU) across animals and images. Violin plots show the distribution of the data. The centre line indicates the median, and the lower and upper bounds indicate the 25th and 75th percentiles, respectively.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Glenn Murray believes Bruno Fernandes will look to leave the club if he doesn’t sign a new Manchester United contract before the January transfer window.
  • Fernandes won the PFA Players’ Player of the Year last year after a superb second half of the season under Michael Carrick, but has not hit those same heights so far this campaign.
  • The Red Devils captain was also dropped for a game after publicly criticising Carrick’s tactics following a heavy Champions League defeat to Como.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Glenn Murray believes Bruno Fernandes will look to leave the club if he doesn’t sign a new Manchester United contract before the January transfer window.

Fernandes won the PFA Players’ Player of the Year last year after a superb second half of the season under Michael Carrick, but has not hit those same heights so far this campaign.

The Red Devils captain was also dropped for a game after publicly criticising Carrick’s tactics following a heavy Champions League defeat to Como.

The arrival of Mauricio Pochettino represents a fresh start for Fernandes this season, but there remains uncertainty over his long-term future at the club given the 32-year-old is out of contract at the end of the season.

Fernandes has already turned down two contract offers from the club, and former Brighton striker Murray believes he could be eyeing up a move away from Old Trafford when the transfer window reopens in January.

‘I wouldn’t burst the bank [on a new contract] for him,’ Murray told Sky Sports. ‘I think he’s not the future of the football club.

‘Listen, he’s given his best years to Manchester United and unfortunately they haven’t won an awful lot, which he would have liked.

‘I think if he gets the option to move on, and it gets to January, and he can start speaking to other people, I think it will open his eyes up to see where he could go and if he could win things and finish off his career more enjoyably, because there have been years at Manchester United that have been really difficult.

‘He has been the standout player, but he is not the future and it could be time to part ways.

Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.

‘It all depends on the salary because if you outlay a lot [on wages], there is nothing coming back on the other end at this point of his career.’.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Pochettino, meanwhile, has confirmed that Fernandes will remain captain under his management and insisted the midfielder is an ‘important’ player for his rebuild.

‘All the players, we were chatting, it was amazing from day one, Bruno is our captain, an important player,’ Pochettino confirmed.

‘But all the players need to think they are crucial, from the bottom to the top.

‘I spent three hours, chatting in my office, with all the players, maybe I miss some injured players. In the next few days, we will talk in an individual way with all of them.

‘It’s important to listen to what they need to say, understand the place they are. Not only on the field, off the field, what’s going on. Some conversations, some collective way, meetings, but focus is on Sunday.’.

Today's Premier League predictions include Arsenal's trip to Newcastle United, and a contest between Manchester City and Fulham.

Seeking to end a three-game losing run in the Premier League, Manchester City welcome Fulham to the Etihad Stadium for Saturday’s lunchtime kickoff.

These two teams last butted heads nine months ago when three first-half goals helped the Citizens claim a comfortable 3-0 home victory.

Maresca will demand a strong reaction from his Man City players following recent setbacks, and their exceptional historical record in this fixture firmly establishes them as the favourites to claim all three points.

While a porous Citizens backline offers encouragement to a Fulham outfit that has drawn a blank in seven of their last 12 Premier League games on the road, we expect the hosts' attacking firepower to comfortably outgun the Cottagers on this occasion.

These two teams served up a nine-goal thriller in the EFL Cup just a couple of months ago, with the West Londoners securing a 6-3 comeback victory in the third round.

Chelsea have not been the same prolific outfit without the presence of Joao Pedro up front, and they could find it difficult to break down a robust Leeds backline without a natural focal point.

Aston Villa's game management has become a growing concern, and Sunderland should fancy their chances of finding the net given that the hosts have failed to keep a clean sheet in any of their last six matches in all competitions.

While the Black Cats will be desperate to build on their victory over Chelsea as they bid to climb away from danger, the absence of both Xhaka and Brobbey is a real blow, and we expect Villa to ultimately navigate their way to a narrow triumph on home soil.

Separated by three places in the Premier League table, 12th-placed Tottenham Hotspur welcome Ipswich Town to the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on Saturday seeking a return to winning ways on matchday 11.

Leeds United halted Spurs' three-match league winning streak before the hiatus, and the capital club now aim to begin a seemingly favourable run of fixtures with a positive result against the Tractor Boys.

Ipswich have scored four goals across their last two away matches, offering encouragement that their varied attacking threats can trouble a Tottenham side carrying several fitness concerns.

Frank's appointment should provide Palace with renewed purpose, but Mateta's suspension and doubts over Sarr and Strand Larsen leave the visitors short of attacking options.

Coventry have scored seven goals across their last three home matches and could exploit the Eagles' defensive uncertainty to spoil the Dane's first assignment.

Eyeing up a place in the top four of the Premier League, in-form Bournemouth welcome Nottingham Forest to the Vitality Stadium on Saturday afternoon.

Both Bournemouth and Forest enter this contest in buoyant mood as they look to build on positive results prior to the international break.

Man Utd make worst start in 40 years after being hauled back by 10-man Spurs

📅 10 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4238 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Manchester United fans were never going to pass up the opportunity to aim a volley of abuse in the direction of their bitter rivals.
  • By the end of another deeply unconvincing performance, though, they were more preoccupied by the problems afflicting their own team than the cheating scandal engulfing Manchester City.
  • Against City at Old Trafford last month, United lost to a team who were down to 10 men after just 23 minutes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Manchester United fans were never going to pass up the opportunity to aim a volley of abuse in the direction of their bitter rivals.

By the end of another deeply unconvincing performance, though, they were more preoccupied by the problems afflicting their own team than the cheating scandal engulfing Manchester City.

Against City at Old Trafford last month, United lost to a team who were down to 10 men after just 23 minutes.

This time around they could not hold on to a lead against a Tottenham Hotspur side also navigating a numerical disadvantage following Rodrigo Bentancur’s sending off.

Rodrigo Bentancur dives in on Luke Shaw and it's all kicking off at Old Trafford! 🫨 https://t.co/uJUAMuZNzc.

The sum total of it all is that United have now made their worst start to a season for 40 years, which is saying something given the traumas of the post-Ferguson era, and perhaps more disconcertingly, look to all intents and purposes like a team going backwards.

The bounce they enjoyed under Michael Carrick last season en route to Champions League qualification is over and, after just six points from as many games, it is hard to shake the feeling that it is going to be anything but a serious battle to finish in the top four or five.

Industry observers note that the supporters did not hide their disgruntlement. There were boos around the half hour mark after an insipid opening when Spurs did everything but score and a slow, sluggish, dishevelled United almost looked impervious to their troubles.

Industry observers note that carrick had called for his players to show some “fire” coming into this match, but instead watched them ambling around like it was all a terrible inconvenience. The ease with which Spurs ran around them was alarming. There were more jeers at the interval and again at full time.

Carrick admitted that “hurt” although not as much you suspect as the sight of players feigning interest and then throwing away three points when they had finally summoned some fight to lead courtesy of Bryan Mbeumo’s goal.

Bryan Mbeumo slots it home to give Manchester United the lead against Spurs! 🎯 https://t.co/7yKnpyhfUe.

It was a lovely finish after good work by the largely anonymous Matheus Cunha, and when Bentancur was sent off five minutes later after butting Luke Shaw, it should have been the cue to see out the game. To fail to do so against a side as toothless as Tottenham made it all the worse. Leading late on against Everton last month, they also failed to get over the line. It cannot keep happening.

In a recent development, equally, United cannot play like they did in the first half here when they face Atlético Madrid in the Spanish capital on Tuesday night or at Elland Road against bitter rivals Leeds five days later and expect to get anything from either game. They are not the sort of matches Carrick would want with his team in this shape, but they need to find some inspiration from somewhere.

Carlos Baleba coming on around the hour mark and making a difference on his debut will at least offer Carrick some grounds for encouragement. The £65m midfield signing from Brighton offers some energy and urgency and looks a more natural bedfellow for Kobbie Mainoo than Youri Tielemans, who was woeful against Spurs and should have come off earlier.

In truth, Tielemans was not alone. Throughout the team there was a disconnect and unease and Carrick admitted it became contagious.

Industry observers note that “We just couldn’t find a way to get ourselves into the game, whether that was with the ball or without the ball,” the United manager remarked. “We were a little bit slow with the decision-making, didn’t quite see the passing areas, the space. You don’t want it to happen, but sometimes it can and it probably spread through the team a little bit too much.”.

It does not help that Bruno Fernandes is being hampered by an injury he has been carrying for weeks or that Carrick has no natural centre-forward to call upon with Benjamin Sesko again sidelined by the recurrence of a worrying shin problem. Amad Diallo did return here after a lengthy lay-off of his own, but did not look match fit.

In defence, Lisandro Martínez did enough to put off Dominic Solanke, who fired over from Sávio’s cross in the second half, but this was otherwise another poor showing from the Argentine centre-back, one of several positions where United need upgrades.

United needed shaking badly, but when Carrick turned to his bench he called upon Joshua Zirkzee, a fitful forward the club wanted to sell this summer, and right-back Diogo Dalot in addition to Baleba.

Recent findings suggest that marcus Rashford cannot have been fit given he was only introduced in the 95th minute and perhaps the same was true of the unused Mason Mount. As for £50m summer signing Andrey Santos, this was another league game when the Brazilian midfielder did not get a look in.

In a recent development, united fans had taunted Spurs when a goal and a man up. “You’re going down with the City,” they crowed, a nod to the possibility of City being expelled or relegated from the Premier League after being found guilty of breaching more than 100 financial rules.

Sources indicate that united fans had also revived their Stretford End “ticker” after reaching the conclusion that none of City’s titles under Abu Dhabi ownership had been won fairly so, in their eyes, it is now 50 years since their rivals last won anything legitimately. City, of course, continue to maintain their innocence and have lodged an appeal.

But United fans were unable to crow for too long once Solanke levelled.

Spurs are level in stoppage-time! 😳 https://t.co/NoivNchgWw.

Sources indicate that it had been similar early in the game when the home fans had trained their sights on City. “You cheating b--------, you know what you are”, they sang lustily.

But as the match wore on, those chants began to quieten as the crowd, taking their lead from the team, fell decidedly flat.

Carrick is going to have to find a spark from somewhere and quickly.

Recent findings suggest that speaking to BBC Match of the Day, Carrick remarked: “It was a mixed game. We found it tough to start with. For a number of reasons, we were not quite there. You could see it was a challenging time.

“But the lads grew into the game, in the second half I thought we were better in everything. To get the game as we wanted it, in such a good position - we should see it through. We have to manage those situations. That’s two late goals which have hurt us, and things look very different. That’s the reality.”.

It has been revealed that when asked about the boos at half-time and full-time, he replied: “It’s not nice, it hurts a lot because I care about this club. But I understand the disappointment, the reality is what it is, we need to get back to winning games.”.

3 - Manchester United have failed to win any of their last three Premier League games against sides that have received a red card (D1 L2). Disadvantage? https://t.co/DuSpvymZfu.

The Tottenham boss told Sky Sports: “I think we played very well against a great team. We had many chances to score in the first half. Three or four. The second half is normal to suffer against this quality. I am very happy because I have seen the right spirit and character.

In a recent development, “We suffered in the game but every situation of the game. I like the situation we were in with the red card. We need this situation. We have not accepted the defeat. We have to react in all ways we can. It is a bad way, it is not the right way. I kiss Bentancur in the dressing room. Football is character.

Sources indicate that “We win the game if we play as a team. We didn’t win this game playing as a team. Every game like today, we will win many games.”.

When asked about Solanke, he replied: “He is a good player for Tottenham. There for not too many strikers better than Solanke. If Manchester City had not entered a legal battle with the Premier League after being found guilty of breaching 114 charges relating to financial regulations by an independent panel, then surely there would be more pressure on the two head coaches in the dugout this evening?

Man Utd and Tottenham have undoubtedly both endured extremely disappointing starts to their respective top-flight campaigns. The hosts sit just inside the bottom half of the table after picking up just five points from their opening five matches. It’s going even worse for Tottenham, who languish in 20th with zero wins and just two points.

The perilous landscape leaves only one reasonable conclusion: this has all the ingredients for an early season six-pointer.

The strain is perhaps less intense on Michael Carrick, with the Englishman having built up a bundle of goodwill after cleaning up the mess left by Ruben Amorim last season as Man Utd eventually finished third, qualifying for the Champions League. Fans were left slightly underwhelmed by the club’s transfer window, with the players at Carrick’s disposal having not forged any momentum so far in this campaign.

It has been revealed that the spotlight is definitely shining more intensely upon Roberto De Zerbi after massive-spending Tottenham splashed over £300m in the summer on the likes of Sandro Tonali, Mateus Fernandes, Jan Paul van Hecke and Savio. However, the Italian boss is yet to strike the correct rhythm with his newly-formed squad. An encouraging performance backed up by a positive result here at Old Trafford could be the perfect antidote to ease the worries of fans fearing that Tottenham could be embroiled in another relegation battle.

All eyes are on this one. Kick-off is at 17:30, with team news coming shortly.
