💡 Key Takeaways
  • Martin’s Day in Germany, a day I’d never heard of until I had a child over here.
  • Martin was, as the story goes, a 4th-Century Roman soldier and is best known for sharing his cloak with a freezing beggar.
  • Industry observers note that fitting, then, that Martin Zubimendi should be linked with a move to Chelsea (and others).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Good morning all, hope you’re well! It’s St. Martin’s Day in Germany, a day I’d never heard of until I had a child over here. Kids will leave Kindergarten and chant as they walk through their neighbourhoods with lanterns this evening, as is tradition. Doesn’t sound creepy at all, does it?

St. Martin was, as the story goes, a 4th-Century Roman soldier and is best known for sharing his cloak with a freezing beggar.

Industry observers note that fitting, then, that Martin Zubimendi should be linked with a move to Chelsea (and others). It would be the saintly thing to do to share some of our midfield spoils with the desperate, downtrodden, shivering squad that Xabi Alonso has at his disposal. I hope we let them get absolutely glacial – Siberian, even, given their history – and keep our glorious cloak of midfielders all to ourselves.

The first rule of the international break is, of course, to ignore all transfer rumours. Club football goes away but there are still pages to fill, newspapers to sell, online traffic to amass, and something has to fill the void.

And, speaking to Marca, the midfielder has denied that he’s unhappy:.

According to recent reports, I’m calm and happy with how I’m handling this situation. (Not playing) is something I’ve never experienced before, and I think you learn from these situations too.

I’m patient. When you’ve been playing a lot of minutes and your role changes to not playing as much, I’m able to see the positive side. I think everything passes, that just like last year the opposite happened to me and I played practically everything, this can change very quickly.

Asked about the toll that playing so much took on him last season – Zubimendi was the only Arsenal player to play in all 38 Premier League games, he started 34 of those and had the third most minutes in the squad, behind David Raya and Declan Rice, across all competitions – he admitted that that was a factor:.

I don’t like to blame everything on my physical condition, but I definitely noticed it that year. It was a fresh year for me, with a lot of new stimuli. I played a huge number of minutes and, to be honest, I was tired. Then there were other things too, but one of them could very well have been my physical condition.

Recent findings suggest that I spoke with Mikel at the beginning of the season. As he does with all the players, he explained the plan to me. He warned me that there were new signings and that there would be playing time for everyone. And here we are, fighting for it.

And he completely dismissed any suggestion that he is talking to other clubs, given those links to the Madrid sides and Chelsea:.

Industry observers note that I haven’t wasted any energy on outside things. I’m busy enough trying to earn a place, get playing time, and fight to win this Premier League, which is looking so promising. I haven’t spent any energy on it, nor have I contacted anyone.

According to recent reports, to be honest, I’m sometimes surprised by the press too. I understand that the winter transfer window is approaching and rumours can surface, but I think we need to be a bit more careful with what we publish. Ultimately, everyone has a team they play for, and we need to respect that. I’ve also read that I might be close (to a transfer), but not at all.

In a recent development, still, I do think the case of Zubimendi is an interesting one. Having lost his place late last season, he returned late in the summer, and is yet to start a Premier League game in 2026-27 following the emergence of Myles Lewis-Skelly and the arrival of Bruno Guimaraes.

Industry observers note that here we have a player Arsenal desperately wanted and agreed a deal for a year ahead of signing him, would they really be looking to move him on again now that he’s spent what is essentially just a quarter of a season not as first choice? So much focus has been placed on building a squad that can sustain injuries or absences, and then we’d leave ourselves light again?

According to recent reports, maybe? You never can know how transfers pan out ahead of time, and things can change quickly in football but, as Zubimendi suggests, they can change quickly in the other direction again too. Did anyone, for instance, envisage Lewis-Skelly starting against Atletico Madrid just a week before it actually happened?

Industry observers note that I do think his particular rise, and a stressful second half of the season, has clouded what we all thought of Zubimendi’s first half-season at Arsenal, and how much he contributed across the entire campaign. At this stage a year ago, we were two points worse off than we are now but still top of the league by six points, with more goals scored and fewer goals conceded than we are 10 games in this time around. He was a substantial part of that.

Industry observers note that he was a huge part of winning the title and reaching the Champions League final – he started 43 of our 53 games across those two competitions. He started every Champions League knockout game up until the semi-final second leg and played all of extra-time in the final.

And if he was suffering physically, there was no break in the summer, as he went off to the World Cup, Spain went all the way, and he was back on the pitch for Arsenal (having had no pre-season) in Cardiff as we won the Community Shield, less than a month on from the World Cup final.

Sources indicate that for all that, I can also see why someone would possibly want to make the case for moving on. Seeing a player not be used (Zubimendi has played in seven of our league games so far this season, by the way!) feels like an obvious place to upgrade, and we’ve been scarred before by letting players sit on the bench before then struggling to move them on for a fair fee.

It has been revealed that we’re also going to need to refresh the age of the team and especially the midfield before long. When you don’t just look at the players themselves but actually account for who is playing the minutes, we have the third-oldest squad in the league this season. The frontline will need newly introduced faces soon – that’s not news to anyone – in terms of age as well as quality, but the midfield will need it on the age front as well.

According to recent reports, we’ve also given the fewest minutes in the league to players under the age of 23 (around 6%) by some distance. If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it, but if you don’t get the balance right it will break in time.

Right now, though, this season, we’re likely to need our whole squad. We can’t be making it weaker. If one of Declan Rice – God forbid – or Bruno Guimaraes were to pick up a knock and miss a month, Zubimendi would suddenly be in line for a lot of football. Zubimendi who, again, was central to us winning the league last season.

In a recent development, it’s far too soon into the season to write his campaign off, especially when we saw how things changed so suddenly in that exact position back in May. Let’s see how things look when the summer rolls around, but there’s no need to rush into a decision.

Recent findings suggest that right then, have a great day all – and I’ll leave you with the gorgeous generosity of another St. Martin close to our hearts.

#83660. The virtues of patience

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arseblog ↗ Open Full Page

The virtues of patience

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1347 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Arseblog

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, it was freezing and wet at the Emirates.
  • It has been revealed that willian was grotesquely slow.
  • According to recent reports, then our captain, Pierre Emerick-Aubameyang, headed a corner into his own net.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Let’s take a journey back in time.

It’s 13 December 2020. Arsenal versus Burnley.

In a recent development, it was freezing and wet at the Emirates. Only 2,000 fans had been allowed in because of Covid, and my mum, my dad, my mate Ben and I made up four of them. We were socially distanced and wearing masks. My glasses kept steaming up.

This was supposed to be fun. Watching my team.

It has been revealed that willian was grotesquely slow. Alex Lacazette was profligate. Rob Holding was bald. Very bald. And Granit Xhaka was angry. So angry, in fact, that in the second half he put his hands around the throat of some opposition goon and, after a VAR review, got himself sent off. There were boos. As many as 2,000 people could muster, anyway.

According to recent reports, then our captain, Pierre Emerick-Aubameyang, headed a corner into his own net. You couldn’t make it up. Except you could. It was the only goal of the game.

By then the steam fogging up my specs might as well have been coming out of my ears. In his player ratings, Andrew M called Xhaka the ‘King of the Idiots’ and described the match and the result as ‘utterly shit’. Which was fair.

It was our seventh defeat in 10 league games and our fourth in a row at home, something that hadn’t happened since 1953. We were 15th, five points above the relegation zone.

It has been revealed that and who was top? Sp*rs. Managed by everyone’s favourite sociopath, Jose Mourinho. Having beaten us in the North London derby the week before, they couldn’t stop gloating.

Recent findings suggest that I’d bought into the Arteta project hook, line and sinker. I still wanted him to be the right man for the job. I was just finding it harder to explain why I thought he was. The FA Cup win had been four months earlier. It felt like years.

The tree, to paraphrase our manager, was shaking.

Industry observers note that it had been shaking for a good two and a half years by then. The soggy bottom of the Arsene Wenger era had left its scars. Those two 3-0 defeats to City in the space of a week still make me wince. Then came the hope that Unai Emery might get us back on track. By the time we’d seen how that played out, I’d got into the habit of talking myself down whenever things looked up. Maybe we’ll get better. Give it time.

In a recent development, the trouble with rock bottom is you never know if there’s another floor below it. Was Burnley ours? I’m still writing about it six years later, so it was probably mine. There were games against Southampton and Everton before Christmas, and I can barely remember either of them.

Industry observers note that then came Boxing Day and a visit from Frank Lampard’s Chelsea. Is it reductive to say that was the day everything changed for Mikel Arteta’s Arsenal? Probably. But my word, watching Bukayo Saka, Emile Smith Rowe and Gabriel Martinelli tear about the place was the fix this addict needed. We went on an unbeaten run after that. Seven whole games! And for the first time in weeks, I was looking forward to what came next.

And here we are in November 2026. Reigning champions of England. Top of the league again. Five points clear. Odds-on favourites to retain the title after 10 games. Sure, throwing hundreds of millions of American dollars at the problem helped. But if there’s a lesson in all this, it’s that hard work and patience pay off.

Which is why I’m using today’s blog to appeal directly to Sir Jim Ratcliffe to give Michael Carrick a stay of execution.

It has been revealed that come on, man, you’re probably still paying off Erik ten Hag and Ruben Amorim, maybe even Ralf Rangnick. Do you really want to go back to the drawing board all over again? Carrick is the man for the Manchester United hot seat. Just look at the way he wore a poppy-embroidered armband as well as a poppy badge at the weekend. The man doesn’t do half measures. He’s a two-scoops guy. Surely that’s something you, a multibillionaire British-born petrochemicals tycoon who lives in Monaco, can get on board with?

I know Mauricio Pochettino might be tempting. He’s got floppy hair, a tan and, despite the Sp*rsy stench, has come to resemble a rather huggable teddy bear. But think it through, Jim. What if he comes in and everybody perks up? It’s much harder to make job cuts and to force out season ticket holders when people are enjoying themselves. Best get through that process first while Michael turns the oil tanker round. It’s not far off, promise, you’re on a two-game unbeaten streak!

According to recent reports, anyway, what would sacking Carrick say about patience? Look at Arteta. There were people who wanted him gone after Burnley and, as you’ve just read, I was close to joining them. Imagine if the club had listened to me. All those years of work, all that progress, all the joy I’ve had watching Arsenal lately. We could have thrown it all away because a man in a damp mask couldn’t see out of his glasses.

According to recent reports, so give Carrick time. Give him January. Give him a full pre-season. And if things still haven’t picked up by this time next year, ask yourself whether one full pre-season, and £100 million on Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos, was ever really enough.

I can only speak for myself, Jim, but I haven’t looked forward to watching Manchester United this much in years.

Right, let’s see if that works….

The Interlull kicks into gear tonight. David Raya, Mikel Merino and Martin Zubimendi are in action for Spain against Czechia, Riccardo Calafiori’s Italy take on France, and England face Croatia at Wembley.

Industry observers note that ezri Konsa and Myles Lewis-Skelly will both miss out at Wembley. Konsa is working on his fitness but will be available to face Spain on Sunday, while our Hale Ender is suspended after picking up two bookings in the Nations League.

Sources indicate that elsewhere, ahead of Sweden’s game against Bosnia and Herzegovina, Viktor Gyokeres has been speaking to the press. Like Martin Zubimendi, he says he’s happy at Arsenal.

“I want to,” he stated, when asked if he’s keen to stay at the Emirates.

“It feels good when I’ve played. We’ve won most of the games. It was a tough loss in the cup (against Fleetwood). Otherwise it’s felt good for myself and the team, indicates the forward. I’ve been doing well lately when I’ve been playing. Right now it feels good.

According to recent reports, “The communication with (Mikel) Arteta is good. We talk about football and how we should play. Before a match, if I’m going to start, we talk about the opponents and what I should think about.”.

He was also asked whether the criticism he gets bothers him.

“Sometimes it might get to me, but overall not so much. If I score goals and assists in the Champions League, I couldn’t care less what they say. It’s nice to do those kinds of performances. To deliver for myself and for the team. That’s where the focus lies.”.

Recent findings suggest that to be fair, I’ve not seen any serious chatter about selling Viktor in January. Whatever you think of him as a player, it would be a strange move unless we’re planning to spend serious money on the attack. And even then it would feel like an unnecessary risk given Kai isn’t exactly pulling up trees and new faces will need an adaptation period.

If he’s happy keeping his head down and doing his bit for the team, I’d keep him around until the summer and reassess then.

It has been revealed that ok. I’m going to leave it there for today. All eyes on Old Trafford, I guess.

In a recent development, A newly introduced Liverpool signing is set to threaten a record-breaking Richard Hughes deal. Liverpool are ready to move on.

Recent findings suggest that if Richard Hughes did anything as Liverpool sporting director, it was strike record-breaking deals. He only actually went all-out in two windows, really, but he broke transfer records in virtually every position.

Of course, the substantial one was Alexander Isak, who became the most expensive player in British football history. That was after signing Florian Wirtz as Liverpool's record signing and first-ever nine-figure transfer.

Another £100m+ signing arrived in 2026: Bradley Barcola. That may or may not be the biggest deal in Liverpool's history, depending on who you ask.

It has been revealed that giovanni Leoni became the most expensive teenager in club history, too. While Hughes also broke Liverpool's record in both full-back positions. It was a spending spree unlike anything we've ever seen before.

And now one of those signings, at least, is under threat.

Sources indicate that sport24 report that Kostas Tsimikas is set to leave Liverpool with the end of his contract next summer. It's an interesting one as this will almost certainly bring a knock-on effect that hits Milos Kerkez.

Kerkez became the most expensive full-back in Liverpool's history when joining from Bournemouth for over £40m. It was a deal that beat the previous record set around a month earlier when Jeremie Frimpong joined.

But Kerkez is yet to fully establish himself. Andoni Iraola actually rotates him with Tsimikas quite heavily and that suggests that any replacement for the Greek left-back would be one that rivals Kerkez for a starting role.

It has been revealed that after all, Liverpool might as well just re-sign Tsimikas if they want a player in a similar role. It only really makes sense to 'upgrade' on him and if that's the case, there would be more minutes available to the arriving star.

Recent findings suggest that tsimikas is already commanding quite a few minutes off of Kerkez as it is. It's entirely possible, in fact, that Liverpool move for a latest left-back who replaces the Hungarian as first-choice, relegating the Hughes signing to backup.

That's the way the wind is blowing, certainly. Kerkez has a lot of time to change things, possibly cementing his role over the rest of the season. If he fails to do that, though, we think his position might be under extreme threat when Liverpool enter the transfer market next summer.

By NATHAN SALT - FOOTBALL REPORTER.

Published: 10:25 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 11:32 EST, 20 November 2026.

Manchester United CEO Omar Berrada insists the team got 'fundamentally better' after this summer's transfer window, as he warned ‘spending just for the sake of it’ is not the route to putting United back on top.

In his first sit-down interview in five months, Berrada tackled topics ranging from the relationship between the Glazers and Ineos, the imminent departure of youngster JJ Gabriel, the decision not to sign a left back in the summer, as well as the decision to push ahead for a latest stadium despite supporter backlash on matchdays.

The United chief has been at the centre of furious protests and anti-ownership chanting at matches this season, alongside Director of Football Jason Wilcox, and he accepted that criticism of United's leadership has, mostly, been fair.

In an interview that aired shortly after newly introduced head coach Mauricio Pochettino spoke to the media for the first time, Berrada was pressed on how much accountability falls at his door with United heading to Anfield this weekend 18th in the Premier League table.

'I think if you think about the fact we've had three permanent managers in less than three seasons, clearly we haven't achieved the stability that we wanted, that's for sure,' Berrada told Sky Sports.

'When it doesn't work out with the coach or the manager, we are all responsible. Myself, the football leadership, everyone who is involved around the coach and the staff and the players. We have to continue improving and getting better.

Manchester United's CEO Omar Berrada finally fronted up in an interview with Sky Sports.

Michael Carrick's sacking was yet another managerial change at United, with the hierarchy under massive scrutiny and Mauricio Pochettino now in the hotseat.

'There are different circumstances why it didn't work out with Erik [ten Hag], and Ruben [Amorim], and now Michael [Carrick], and we are always learning and, as I stated, trying to improve and understand what has failed.

'The challenge is we're trying to find the right manager for the squad that we have with a specific set of skills in that moment to make them perform at their best level.

'It's true, we have to accept the criticism that we haven't been able to achieve that stability with one coach and our aim is to do that as soon as possible. Of course, we hope now that Mauricio coming in will give us that stability that I think we all need.'.

Berrada's links to Manchester City, where he worked prior to joining United, were brought up, not least given he worked at the club during the period that City have had charges brought against them.

'I'm not concerned,' Berrada insisted.

But at his fresh home there are challenges aplenty, not least having got another managerial appointment wrong, sacking Carrick less than six months after handing him a two-year deal, and so it was put to Berrada: is the club actually progressing?

'It's not good enough, not acceptable and that's why we've made the change that we made so that we can move forward,' he concluded.

(L-R) Sir Jim Ratcliffe, Berrada and Jason Wilcox have drawn plenty of ire from Man United fans.

'But we are laying the foundations for sustained growth, to put us in a position where we can be competitive consistently. It's not always been that.

'Last year we finished third, we were happy with the squad, we were happy with the way we were going. And now, a few months later, we are not where we need to be. But the foundations are there and I am convinced that we are heading in the right direction. Very positive.'.

  • I always had my doubts, not least because your style of play is always defined by your talent.
  • In attacking areas, he had talent, even if it wasn’t balanced.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, there was a lot of speculation as to how Arsenal might change this season having flung a 22-year-old monkey (how long do monkeys live for?!) from their back in May by finally winning a league title. Would lifting the Premier League trophy lead to a new era of more expressive, urbane football?

I always had my doubts, not least because your style of play is always defined by your talent. Most of Arsenal’s elite talent is behind the ball. Arteta didn’t build Arsenal from the defence first, in my view, because he felt specifically that was the best way. It was just the area of the team that required the most attention when he was appointed.

In attacking areas, he had talent, even if it wasn’t balanced. Aubameyang, Lacazette and Pepe with Saka and Martinelli coming to the boil was a good collection of talent, even if the pieces didn’t always fit neatly together. The list of defenders he inherited included Mustafi, Sokratis, Holding, Chambers, Kolasinac and Mari. That’s why he went defence first, broadly speaking.

The moves the club have tried to make in recent seasons, especially this summer, shows you that Arteta wants his attack to be sharper than it is. For reasons I won’t relitigate here, the club were not able to add a number of high end attacking targets. Which means once again, Arsenal are reliant on Arteta’s coaching talents to squeeze more juice from the orange. Here are three things that have jumped out at me this season.

Industry observers note that arsenal spent a lot of money on Bruno Guimaraes this season and I will come onto some of the reasons why in the next section. But that signing has given Arteta a deep well of central options, with Rice, Bruno, Lewis Skelly, Odegaard, Merino and Zubimendi part of this midfield menagerie.

Arsenal use these options interchangeably and often according to game state. Art de Roche of the Athletic went into how Arteta has used the divergent profiles of Myles Lewis Skelly and Bruno Guimaraes so far in this campaign. In home games against Leeds and Everton, Lewis Skelly got the nod from the start.

Recent findings suggest that in away games at Nottingham Forest and Liverpool, Bruno’s more robust approach was favoured. The pair have made significant impacts from the bench too. When the 1-0 victory at Anfield had become a little too ‘basketball’, Lewis Skelly came on and provided calm assurance in possession.

According to recent reports, when the Gunners needed a little more belligerence away at Sunderland, Bruno came on and larruped the ball into the top corner from 25 yards. However, Arteta didn’t part with a significant part of his summer budget for a 28-year-old (he turns 29 next week but, for now, he remains 28 because that’s how it works) to be a high level rotation option.

Against Hull City last weekend, Bruno was selected and he played deeper than Declan Rice and Martin Odegaard. As Adrian Clarke pointed out in his match analysis piece, Bruno passed the ball to Odegaard 25 times in that match and the pair exchanged 35 passes in total. The idea was clear, to use Bruno’s punchiness in possession a little lower to feed Odegaard.

Against Everton, Mikel Merino was selected in midfield and Lewis Skelly started at left-back. I think this was about more than mere rotation. Arteta always highly respects the aerial capabilities of David Moyes’ Everton team, which makes sense since he played in a David Moyes Everton team for such a long time.

In 2023-24, Arteta selected Fabio Vieira ahead of Kai Havertz in midfield at Goodison Park because he wanted to keep the ball on the floor (Arsenal won that game 1-0 via a short corner routine because they did not see the logic of aerial corners against a team like Everton).

In a recent development, last season at the Hill Dickinson Arsenal enjoyed a season high for passes attempted and completed because they wanted to keep the ball on the floor and avoid transitions. Arteta has a carousel available to him in midfield and a different club in the bag depending on what is called for on the day.

Per Opta, Arsenal have been caught offside 35 times so far this season, at least 11 more times than any other team. That rate of 3.5 offsides per game is the highest of any Premier League team since 2009. Kai Havertz has been flagged 15 times now, the next highest offender in the league is Dominic Calvert-Lewin with eight. Opta provide a deeper dive on those numbers here.

Recent findings suggest that so what does this tell us, aside from the fact that Havertz needs to work on his timing? It means that Arsenal are far more willing to go in behind and they are willing to test the opposition backline earlier in moves. This was a substantial part of the reason they signed Bruno in the first place, Arteta wants to play with the risk reward dial with the ball.

According to recent reports, havertz also hasn’t been quite good enough to finish some of those one v one situations when he has got in behind the opponent’s back line. He fluffed his lines against Hull last weekend and in the 3-0 defeat at Brighton, he blasted his effort straight at the Brighton keeper when put through one v one.

Industry observers note that but here, I will express my usual caveat, we need to normalise strikers missing chances and focus more on process than outcome. Most chances are missed, you want to worry when your striker is getting few shots. There have also been nascent signs that Arsenal have been using Gyokeres well in some of these situations.

That Havertz chance at the Amex was created by Gyokeres taking one touch with his back to goal and hooking the ball past the committed defensive line. Gyokeres did much the same for Madueke in Prague. It seems like Arsenal have worked on getting Gyokeres to use his physicality to initially retain the ball- something he badly struggled with last season- but creating situations where he can release it swiftly.

Arsenal’s out of possession prowess is one thing that has been a constant from last season. It is Arsenal’s superpower, so even when they can only manage one goal, it is usually enough to take maximum points. To retain their superpower, Arsenal changed to stay the same, if that makes sense.

Recent findings suggest that the signing of Ezri Konsa from Aston Villa was questioned by many but his presence has made the absence of a world class centre-back like William Saliba a sidebar, which is quite a feat. Arsenal ostensibly took William Saliba’s pizza chart and looked for the most Saliba like defender they could find and bought Konsa.

The loss of Saliba ought to have offered an enormous threat to Arsenal’s defensive stability. Arsenal’s tactical organisation out of possession is elite but so too are the individuals that helm it. Raya, Saliba, Gabriel and Rice are among the best players in the world in their respective positions.

Industry observers note that taking out one of those pillars ought to have derailed Arsenal’s defensive stability and it hasn’t because Konsa has the quality and poise to retain the team’s biggest strength. His pass completion stats are Saliba-esque and the quality of not giving the ball away needlessly is a significant part of the Gunners’ meanness.

It has been revealed that how much Arsenal could improve in attack without significant additions was an unknown so Arteta could not afford to sacrifice the team’s defensive ceiling while he plays with those levers. The addition of Konsa was a personnel change that allowed Arsenal to remain the same.

By Naim Beneddra | 21 Nov 2026 12:05, Last updated: 21 Nov 2026 12:06.

Tottenham Hotspur are reportedly tracking one of French football's most prolific young players, but could face a significant financial obstacle and an unusual transfer arrangement if they pursue a January deal.

Roberto De Zerbi's side have identified Stade de Reims midfielder Yaya Fofana as a potential target, with scouts expected to attend Saturday's Ligue 2 encounter against Saint-Etienne to assess the 22-year-old in person.

Sources indicate that according to Foot Mercato, Tottenham are impressed by the Ivory Coast international's remarkable start to the season. However, Reims are unwilling to lose their leading attacking performer midway through their promotion campaign and would reportedly demand more than €25m (£22m).

The French club could nevertheless consider a deal allowing Fofana to remain on loan until the summer, potentially enabling interested teams to secure his signature without immediately removing him from Nicolas Usai's squad.

Fofana's emergence is particularly striking given that he spent more than a year on the sidelines between 2025 and 2026 after suffering a serious stress fracture.

Industry observers note that the former Lens youngster has returned in outstanding form, benefiting from Usai's decision to deploy him further forward. Although naturally a midfielder capable of operating in defensive and central positions, he has developed into Reims' principal attacking threat.

Fofana has scored 11 goals and provided two assists in 12 Ligue 2 appearances, placing him at the top of the division's goalscoring charts despite not being a conventional centre-forward.

In a recent development, his finishing efficiency is equally remarkable. Of his 19 shots on target, 11 have resulted in goals, while his tally considerably exceeds his expected-goals figure of 4.9. That represents an overperformance of 6.1 goals, although maintaining such clinical finishing throughout the campaign would be difficult.

Earlier this month, Fofana also received his first Ivory Coast call-up, marking another significant milestone following his lengthy injury absence.

Sources indicate that tottenham reportedly admire his versatility and attacking output, while Foot Mercato claims that the player is attracted by the prospect of competing in England. Saturday's encounter with Ligue 2 leaders Saint-Etienne offers Spurs' scouts an opportunity to assess him against strong opposition.

Despite the growing interest, Reims are determined to retain Fofana for the remainder of their promotion campaign.

According to Foot Mercato, the French club would not accept less than the €25m (£22m) received from Patrick Zabi's recent sale, with Fofana's performances strengthening their negotiating position.

An immediate January departure is reportedly off the table, although a transfer followed by a six-month loan back to Reims could provide a compromise. Tottenham would secure a long-term investment, while the French side would retain a crucial player for the decisive months of the season.

Industry observers note that competition could complicate matters. Galatasaray have also been linked with Fofana, while Stuttgart and Trabzonspor are reportedly monitoring his progress.

In a recent development, reims' negotiating position is strengthened by the midfielder's long-term contract. Several reports list its expiry as June 2030, although the club's most recent publicly confirmed extension, revealed in November 2024, ran until June 2029.

Sources indicate that for Tottenham, scouting remains the expected next step. No offer has been confirmed, and there is no indication of an agreement with Reims or the player.

Fofana's impressive performances have made him one of Ligue 2's standout players, but Reims' insistence on keeping him until the summer means that any interested club must decide whether securing an early agreement justifies an investment exceeding £22m.

Conservation of the tumour microenvironment across organs and species

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 90 min read (18005 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~90 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Current understanding of the host tissue response to solid tumours is largely based on investigations of tumour types in isolation1.
  • Solid-organ cancers represent a complex spectrum of pathology, with the intricately associated TME having a pivotal role in disease progression and therapeutic response4,5.
  • Previous studies have identified distinct cell subpopulations within the TME based on their gene expression profiles, spatial distributions and functional characteristics17,18,19,20,21.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Current understanding of the host tissue response to solid tumours is largely based on investigations of tumour types in isolation1. Given the breadth and diversity of human tumour pathology and contributions of tumour microenvironment (TME) cells to disease progression, pan-cancer analysis is needed to bridge major themes of stromal and immune cell evolution. To date, however, efforts to compare the TME response across cancers have been limited in scope2,3. Here we conduct a comprehensive pan-cancer analysis by algorithmically screening thousands of publicly available single-cell transcriptomic datasets for stromal and immune signatures across species and tissue types. We demonstrate conserved hallmarks of host cell transcriptional programming in response to malignancy across 42 cancer types in more than 2,000 human and mouse tumour samples. These findings are codified as an interactive web atlas (tmeatlas.stanford.edu) and software package (scTME) that will serve as practical resources for the systematic interrogation of the TME in tumours.

Solid-organ cancers represent a complex spectrum of pathology, with the intricately associated TME having a pivotal role in disease progression and therapeutic response4,5. Within the TME, both stromal and immune cells have emerged as key modulators of tumour growth, invasion and metastasis1,6,7,8,9,10. However, different studies (often in single-organ contexts) have shown conflicting roles for these cells in promoting versus suppressing tumour growth11,12,13,14. The heterogeneity of the TME, both within individual tumours and across tumour types, poses a substantial challenge to understanding the functional diversity of tumour-associated stromal and immune cells3,15,16.

Previous studies have identified distinct cell subpopulations within the TME based on their gene expression profiles, spatial distributions and functional characteristics17,18,19,20,21. However, these findings stem largely from isolated single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) studies22,23,24, and subsequent pan-cancer efforts have remained limited in size and scope3,25,26,27,28. To our knowledge, the largest cancer-associated fibroblast atlas to date integrates data from 1,116 samples across 10 tumour types29; the largest tumour endothelial cell atlas includes 575 samples across 19 tumour types30; and no specific tumour mural or nerve atlases have been generated. Pan-cancer immune cell atlases have been larger28, especially those focused on individual immune cell lineages31,32,33; however, these typically have not examined immune cell interactions within the broader TME.

Here we integrated single-cell transcriptomic data from 3,381 human and mouse samples across 42 cancer types and 258 datasets to create a definitive TME transcriptional atlas. By mapping this massive cellular landscape, we resolved the stromal and immune ecosystem of solid tumours. Furthermore, by linking enriched subpopulations to poor clinical outcomes, we identified opportunities for future TME-targeted cancer therapies. Key computational predictions are subsequently validated through in vitro and in vivo experiments. Finally, we have consolidated this work into an interactive web atlas (tmeatlas.stanford.edu) and R software package (scTME) that will serve as practical resources for groups investigating the TME.

To systematically analyse single-cell transcriptomic data, we evaluated every scRNA-seq cancer study published in the public domain between January 2014 and July 2025. Separate queries were evaluated independently for human and mouse datasets within the foundational public repositories for single-cell transcriptomics: the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) and ArrayExpress. We screened a total of 3,975 published datasets (Fig. 1a). Studies specific to either blood or central nervous system cancers were excluded from our analysis, as were those failing to meet specific architectural requirements (Methods; see Fig. 1a,b). Our comprehensive screen identified 190 human and 68 mouse datasets (Supplementary Table 1), collectively comprising more than 15.4 million cells. Collectively, these datasets formed the final analytical cohort, comprising 3,381 individual scRNA-seq samples across 42 unique cancer types (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Tables 2 and 3).

Industry observers note that a, Systematic workflow detailing the scRNA-seq dataset curation process. The initial screen examined 3,975 datasets, of which 190 human and 68 mouse scRNA-seq remained after filtering. The combined 258 datasets comprised 3,381 samples and more than 15 million cells. Schematic created in BioRender; Wang, H. https://biorender.com/w8x4pii (2026). CNS, central nervous system. b, Illustration of all cancer types from human (top) and mouse (bottom) included in this study. HNSCC, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma; MPNST, malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour; NSCLC, non-small-cell lung cancer; SCLC, small-cell lung cancer. Illustration created in BioRender; Wang, H. https://biorender.com/p0byno1 (2026).

To process the more than 12.8 million human cells from 2,855 samples and 190 datasets (Extended Data Fig. 1a,b and Supplementary Fig. 1), nearly an order of magnitude greater than many recent seminal studies3,25,26,27,28,31,32,33,34, we used sketch-based sampling and memory read optimization (Extended Data Fig. 1c,d). We applied three independent approaches for data integration to reduce batch effects: Harmony, scVI and FastMNN (Extended Data Figs. 1e and 2a). We then projected each integrated result onto the full dataset (Extended Data Fig. 2b,c). Supervised annotation using four methods—canonical marker genes, estimated copy number variation (inferCNV), SingleR and scATOMIC (Extended Data Fig. 3 and Supplementary Fig. 2)—delineated the presence of seven main cell types across nearly all human cancers (Fig. 2a–c, Extended Data Fig. 1e,f and Supplementary Table 4). These encompass principal stromal (fibroblast, endothelial, mural and nerve) and immune (myeloid and lymphoid) lineages, alongside epithelial cells, which were excluded from subsequent characterization to focus on the two core TME compartments. Comparing the three integration approaches (Supplementary Table 5), Harmony demonstrated the most robust integration and was selected for all subsequent evaluations. The three integration approaches also frequently yielded discordant cell-type assignments for individual cells (Extended Data Fig. 2d–f), highlighting the stochasticity and misclassification risks inherent to relying on any single method35,36. To mitigate this, we provisionally pooled all cells assigned to a specific TME lineage by any of the three algorithms (Extended Data Fig. 1g). Misassigned cells within these overlapping pools were subsequently removed through recursive downstream filtering (Extended Data Fig. 1h and Supplementary Fig. 3a–e), generating final, high-fidelity atlases for the six principal TME cell types (Fig. 2d–i and Extended Data Fig. 1i,j).

In a recent development, a, UMAP embeddings of 12,855,771 cells from 190 human studies integrated using Harmony, with consensus seven cell-type annotations (outlined and labelled within the panel) derived through multiple annotation approaches (Extended Data Figs. 1 and 2 and Supplementary Figs. 1–3). Individual cells are labelled according to downstream final cell annotations in panels d–i. cDC, conventional dendritic cell; DC, dendritic cell; End, endothelial; Fib, fibroblast; Lym, lymphoid; Mac, macrophage; mem, memory; Mono, monocyte; mregDC, mature dendritic cell enriched in immunoregulatory molecules; Mur, mural; myel, myelinating; Myl, myeloid; Neut, neutrophil; NK, natural killer; SMC, smooth muscle cell; TFH, follicular helper T; Treg, regulatory T. b, Total number of human samples included for each type of cancer. c, Distribution of cell types for each cancer, after selecting for only unsorted samples. Abbreviations of cancer names are listed in Supplementary Table 2. d, UMAP embedding of CAFs, manually clustered into four parent populations (outlined and labelled within the UMAP) from a total of seven transcriptionally distinct subpopulations, the latter of which are coloured separately (top left). A dot plot displaying relative gene expression for characteristic markers of the seven transcriptionally distinct CAF subpopulations shown in the left panel (top right). Distributions of CAF subpopulations among tumour samples for different cancer types are also shown (bottom; n = 328,877 cells). e–i, UMAPs (top left), dot plots (top right) and distributions among tumour samples for different cancer types (bottom) for endothelial (e; n = 234,948 cells), mural (f; n = 162,178 cells), nerve (g; n = 7,655 cells), lymphoid (h; n = 1,580,785 cells) and myeloid (i; n = 805,111 cells) cells. Between 3 and 12 subpopulations are identified for each cell type, and one population-defining gene per subpopulation is displayed in the dot plot for each cell type (full list in Supplementary Tables 6 and 7).

We next characterized cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), the predominant stromal population in the TME37. Following our recursive isolation strategy (Extended Data Fig. 1h), we delineated four transcriptionally distinct CAF meta-clusters (Fig. 2d) expressing canonical markers (PDGFRA, LUM and DCN) and lacking non-fibroblast markers (Extended Data Fig. 4a and Supplementary Fig. 4). Specifically, we identified (1) antigen-presenting CAFs (apCAFs; class II HLA+), (2) immunomodulatory/inflammatory CAFs (iCAFs; cytokine+), (3) myofibroblastic/mechanoresponsive CAFs (mCAFs; extracellular matrix (ECM)+, mechanotransduction+), and (4) steady-state CAFs (ssCAFs; progenitor-like markers+; Fig. 2d), broadly consistent with observations from our previous work38 and that of others25,39,40,41. High-resolution sub-clustering (Fig. 2d, Supplementary Table 6 and 7 and Supplementary Fig. 4) further stratified these into seven subpopulations: two iCAF (CXCL8+ or ISG15+), two mCAF (LRRC15+ or COL4A1+), two ssCAF (PI16+ or CXCL14+) and one apCAF. All seven subpopulations were conserved across nearly all evaluated tumour types and tissues (Fig. 2d, bottom). Of note, apCAFs were nearly universally present, whereas previous studies had found them only in rare tumour subsets6. Furthermore, the human apCAFs that we identified did not express mesothelial markers such as MSLN, which are characteristic of mouse apCAFs42 (Extended Data Fig. 4a).

Comparing relative abundances between tumour and non-malignant tissues (Fig. 3a), both mCAF populations were significantly enriched in tumours (3.5-fold for LRRC15+; 2.7-fold for COL4A1+; Supplementary Table 8), reflecting cancer-induced desmoplasia37,43. Similarly, iCAFs and apCAFs were enriched in tumour samples (6.3-fold for ISG15+ iCAFs, 1.3-fold for CXCL8+ iCAFs and 2.0-fold for apCAFs), consistent with their roles in inducing immune evasion42 or secreting inflammatory cytokines41. Analysing abundance across tumour stage and patient treatment response, we found ISG15+ iCAFs, LRRC15+ mCAFs and COL4A1+ mCAFs significantly enriched in late-stage (III–IV) versus early-stage (I–II) tumours (1.9-fold, 1.3-fold and 1.2-fold, respectively; Fig. 3b). Treatment responsiveness did not significantly correlate with any CAF subpopulation (Fig. 3c). Overall, ISG15+ iCAFs were the most consistently enriched fibroblast subset defining both the malignant state and advanced disease (Fig. 3a–c, blue box).

Focusing on the iCAF compartment, our atlas revealed two distinct and conserved transcriptional states: ISG15+ iCAFs exhibiting canonical interferon-γ (IFNγ) stimulation (for example, CXCL10)44, and CXCL8+ iCAFs expressing pro-inflammatory cytokines (for example, CXCL1)41. Crucially, these iCAF subpopulations provide additional granularity compared with previously reported CXCL12+ iCAFs39. Recent consensus frameworks have identified CXCL12 to be among the steady-state fibroblast hallmark genes rather than specific to a malignancy-induced inflammatory CAF state25. In line with this, our CXCL14+ ssCAFs co-expressed high levels of CXCL12 while maintaining a homeostatic signature. Abundance analyses revealed divergent ssCAF dynamics: conventional PI16+ ssCAFs (which also strongly express CXCL12) were heavily enriched in non-malignant tissue (2.8-fold), potentially representing a progenitor pool, whereas the CXCL14+ pool remained proportionally stable across benign and malignant tissues (1.0-fold), typifying embedded parenchymal fibroblasts. We therefore propose that traditional ‘CXCL12+ iCAFs’ are more accurately classified as tissue-resident CXCL14+ ssCAFs.

Recent findings suggest that to elucidate the regulatory networks driving these distinct states, we examined transcription factor activity using SCENIC. The apCAF population exhibited elevated inferred activity of RUNX3 and IKZF1, regulators of MHC class II expression45, suggesting a mechanism for direct T cell interaction and immunotherapy resistance (Extended Data Fig. 5a). The ISG15+ iCAFs indicated predicted activation of ETV7 and IRF2, implicating suppressive cytokine signalling in tumour progression46 (Extended Data Fig. 5b). Both mCAF populations were enriched for CREB3L1 and NKX3-2, linked to ECM overexpression and stiffness (Extended Data Fig. 5c). Conversely, ssCAF populations exhibited higher predicted activity of CEBPA and FOXO3, which regulate lineage and redox homeostasis, respectively, consistent with the homeostatic properties ascribed to this population26 (Extended Data Fig. 5d). Overall, these regulatory profiles broadly align with the putative functional roles attributed to each CAF subpopulation.

In a recent development, to evaluate whether specific populations could be distinguished by differences in metabolic programs, we applied scMetabolism to analyse our scRNA-seq dataset. Of note, we observed that LRRC15+ mCAFs were enriched for genes associated with elevated oxidative phosphorylation, in contrast to the traditional glycolytic programs of ISG15+ iCAFs (Extended Data Fig. 5e,f and Supplementary Fig. 5a–c). These profiles align with the distinct energy demands of each cell type: iCAFs expressed genes linked with rapid glycolytic ATP generation that would permit overproduction of pro-inflammatory cytokines, whereas mCAFs were predicted to utilize the more efficient oxidative phosphorylation, enabling them to sustain intense ECM production and remodelling driving the desmoplastic response to neoplasia47. ssCAFs exhibited globally lower expression of metabolic pathway genes, reinforcing their relatively quiescent state.

To determine whether these distinct functional and metabolic states ultimately impact patient survival, we paired bulk RNA-seq and clinical outcome data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) using CIBERSORTx deconvolution (Supplementary Table 9 and Supplementary Fig. 6a,b). Patients whose tumours were estimated to have higher abundances of apCAFs, iCAFs or mCAFs exhibited worse overall survival across most cancer types, consistent with previous observations48. By contrast, we observed a positive (but not statistically significant; 1.3-fold, P = 0.27) relationship between CXCL14+ ssCAF proportion and patient survival. Together, these results suggest that fibroblast differentiation and lineage progression may be associated with worse outcomes in solid-organ tumours, reflecting a pro-tumorigenic role for apCAFs, iCAFs and mCAFs.

Industry observers note that beyond fibroblasts, we examined tumour endothelial, mural and nerve cells, which drive angiogenesis, cytokine signalling and metastatic spread1,7,8,49. In silico isolation of endothelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 1a–j) identified five pan-cancer subpopulations (Fig. 2e): GJA5+ arterial, CA4+ capillary, PROX1+ lymphatic, ESM1+ tip and ACKR1+ venous. All expressed canonical markers (PECAM1, VWF and CDH5) and lacked non-endothelial signatures (Extended Data Fig. 4b, Supplementary Table 6 and Supplementary Fig. 7). Of note, angiogenic ESM1+ tip cells50 were the sole endothelial subpopulation significantly enriched in tumours versus non-malignant tissue (1.7-fold; Fig. 3a and Supplementary Table 8), reflecting dysfunctional tumour neovascularization51. These tip cells, co-expressing FLT1 (VEGFR1) and KDR (VEGFR2), were significantly elevated in treatment non-responsive tumours (1.9-fold; Fig. 3c). Furthermore, they correlated with elevated metabolic activity (Extended Data Fig. 5g and Supplementary Fig. 5d) and worse overall survival across most TCGA cohorts (Supplementary Fig. 6b). These data reinforce the pro-tumorigenic role of tip cells7,52,53, which may continuously support growth by rapidly initiating marginal angiogenesis, highlighting them as candidate targets for multi-drug therapy.

Sources indicate that subclustering of pan-cancer mural cells delineated six distinct subpopulations (Fig. 2f): CCL2+, CD248+ and ISG15+ pericytes; RERGL+ and WFDC1+ vascular smooth muscle cells; and DES+ visceral smooth muscle cells. All expressed canonical markers (RGS5, PDGFRB and CSPG4) and lacked non-mural signatures (Supplementary Table 6 and Supplementary Fig. 8). ISG15+ and CD248+ pericytes, alongside WFDC1+ vascular smooth muscle cells, were significantly enriched in tumours versus non-malignant tissue (4.5-fold, 1.8-fold and 1.2-fold, respectively; Fig. 3a and Supplementary Table 8), with ISG15+ pericytes also exhibiting elevated overall metabolic activity (Extended Data Fig. 5h). Clinically, CD248+ pericytes correlated with poor treatment response (1.8-fold; Fig. 3c). Mechanistically, both tumour-enriched pericyte populations expressed ECM genes (COL1A1, COL3A1 and COL4A1), supporting a role in tumour desmoplasia (Supplementary Fig. 5e,f). Of note, PIEZO2, which encodes a mechanotransduction channel, was detected in a small subset of CD248+ pericytes and was not detected in other mural populations (Supplementary Fig. 8). Detection was sparse and expression levels were low, indicating selective rather than robust population-specific expression. Given the established role of PIEZO2 in cellular mechanosensation54, we hypothesize that this fraction of pro-fibrotic pericytes may be activated by the stiffened TME to further upregulate ECM production, a possibility that merits further investigation.

According to recent reports, finally, we analysed tumour-associated nerve cells, filtering out neural crest cancers to avoid transcriptional overlap with nerve-based tumours49. Our analysis revealed three distinct subpopulations and their canonical markers: MLANA+ melanocytes, MPZ+ myelinating Schwann cells and NGFR+ non-myelinating Schwann cells (Fig. 2g, Supplementary Table 6 and Supplementary Fig. 9). Subpopulation proportions varied markedly across tumour types (Fig. 2g, bottom). Because this heterogeneity probably reflects both tissue-specific neural architecture and the general rarity of nerve cells in standard biopsies, these populations were omitted from subsequent downstream analyses.

According to recent reports, comprising over 2.4 million cells, immune cells constituted the largest TME compartment in our atlas. In silico isolation broadly segregated these into lymphoid and myeloid lineages. Focusing first on lymphoid cells—primary mediators of antitumour immunity55—we identified 11 subpopulations: CD4+ (3) and CD8+ (3) T cells, natural killer cells (1), B cells (3) and plasma cells (1; Fig. 2h, Supplementary Table 6 and Supplementary Fig. 10). Nearly all T cell populations were significantly enriched in tumours (Fig. 3a). This was driven primarily by CD8+ISG15+ IFN-primed T cells (2.4-fold) and CD8+GZMB+ tumour-reactive exhausted T (TEX) cells (1.5-fold). Of note, this GZMB+ population was also significantly enriched in early-stage disease (Fig. 3b), reflecting an initial wave of localized antitumour immunity undergoing rapid, chronic antigen-driven dysfunction56. In addition, FOXP3+ regulatory T cells (1.8-fold) and CXCL13+ follicular helper T cells (1.6-fold) were both enriched in tumours. By contrast, B cell and plasma populations were comparatively depleted within the tumour but enriched in non-malignant tissue, probably reflecting peritumoural accumulation and immune exclusion from the tumour core57.

Examining tumour myeloid cells, we identified dendritic cells (three populations), monocytes (two populations), macrophages (four populations), mast cells, neutrophils and osteoclasts (Fig. 2i, Supplementary Table 6 and Supplementary Fig. 11). Most spanned all tumour types, except the tissue-specific osteoclasts (Fig. 2i, bottom). Three macrophage subtypes and LAMP3+ mature immunoregulatory dendritic cells were significantly tumour enriched (Fig. 3a), with SPP1+ and MARCO+ subpopulations further enriched in late-stage disease (Fig. 3b). SPP1+ macrophages (GPNMB+ and APOC1+) are known drivers of desmoplasia and poor clinical outcomes32, whereas late-stage MARCO+ enrichment suggests a specialized role in immunosuppression and hindered phagocytosis. Conversely, C1QC+ macrophages maintain a homeostatic, complement-rich signature (C1QA–C and FOLR2) linked to T cell infiltration and a non-exhausted TME58. LAMP3+ mature immunoregulatory dendritic cells (IDO1+ and CCR7+) represent a critical regulatory checkpoint, limiting cytotoxic T cell activity to facilitate late-stage immune evasion59. Finally, shared ISG15+ ‘IFN-primed’ clusters across both macrophages and T cells suggest a common axis of chronic inflammation driving terminal exhaustion via sustained type I IFN signalling31,32.

To evaluate alignment with broader transcriptional consensus models, we performed quantitative cell-level comparisons against four pan-cancer reference atlases using pairwise expression mapping via our scTME software package60 (Extended Data Fig. 6a–d). Most of our subpopulations exhibited strong, reciprocal alignment with comparable cell types across datasets (for example, PI16+ ssCAFs, LRRC15+ mCAFs, ESM1+ tip cells, C1QC+/SPP1+ macrophages and FOXP3+ regulatory T cells). These comparisons also differentiated several of our newly characterized and finely partitioned subpopulations. The IFN-primed (ISG15+) axis mapped robustly to analogous IFN-activated states across lineages (Extended Data Fig. 6b). In addition, our newly identified ISG15+ pericytes mapped to parent pericytes (Extended Data Fig. 6a) but diverged from CD248+ pericytes in broader TME atlases by lacking myofibroblast overlap, reinforcing their distinct state (Extended Data Fig. 6c,d). Furthermore, CXCL14+ fibroblasts mapped predominantly to non-inflammatory populations—unlike the CXCL8+ and ISG15+ iCAF subpopulations—supporting their separation from canonical iCAFs. Overall, although our TME atlas is broadly congruent with established datasets, our fibroblast and mural subpopulations reflect a uniquely refined, data-driven partitioning with functional relevance.

It has been revealed that our meta-analysis identified apCAFs across nearly all evaluated tumour types (Fig. 2d, bottom), far exceeding the limited number of cancers in which they have been validated in vivo6. Therefore, we performed immunohistochemistry to confirm their presence in previously uncharacterized tumour types. Co-staining for the membranous fibroblast marker PDGFRα and the antigen-presenting marker HLA-DR confirmed apCAF presence in human pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) controls61, as well as in previously non-validated colorectal cancer (CRC) and papillary thyroid cancer (PTC) tissues, as predicted by our atlas (Fig. 3d). To exclude possible immune cell misclassification, we analysed multiplexed spatial proteomic (CODEX) data from human PDAC62. Spindle-like HLA-DR+ cells localized to highly fibrotic (COL1A1+/αSMA+) regions, lacked immune or epithelial markers (Fig. 3g,h), and occupied distinct ECM architectures associated with poor patient outcomes (Fig. 3e,f and Supplementary Fig. 12a–f). We further orthogonally validated apCAF presence using public Xenium spatial transcriptomic datasets63,64 (Supplementary Fig. 13a–c). scRNA-seq revealed only a modest correlation between apCAF and T cell abundances in tumour samples (Supplementary Fig. 14a), suggesting that apCAF expansion occurs regional to but independent of direct T cell support. By contrast, ISG15+ iCAFs strongly correlated with CD8+ISG15+ IFN-primed T cells (Supplementary Fig. 14b), supporting our hypothesis that this CAF population interacts with T cells to drive exhaustion and promote immune evasion.

To infer interaction networks, we paired CellChat receptor–ligand predictions with orthogonal NicheNet modelling of downstream transcriptional targets. Because multiple lineages harboured ISG15+ clusters, we first evaluated the IFNγ network. CellChat predicted robust signalling from CD8+GZMB+ tumour-reactive TEX cells to ISG15+ iCAFs (Fig. 4a), which was corroborated by NicheNet (Fig. 4b). These aligned predictions support the hypothesis that ISG15+ iCAFs act as direct responders to chronic, T cell-derived IFNγ within the TME. Applying this approach to explore drivers of dysfunctional neovascularization, CellChat predicted that ESM1+ endothelial tip cells receive disproportionately high VEGF signalling from tumour-associated macrophages and monocytes (Extended Data Fig. 7a). NicheNet further corroborated this relationship (Extended Data Fig. 7b), successfully recapitulating this established myeloid-driven angiogenic axis using data solely from our atlas65. Conversely, NicheNet did not directly substantiate several other CellChat-predicted receptor–ligand pairings as transcriptional drivers, suggesting that these specific interactions may operate via indirect or non-transcriptional mechanisms (Extended Data Fig. 7c,d and Supplementary Fig. 15a–d).
